speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
My motion is based on the fact that the organization and implementation of plans for the 1976 Olympics are obviously out of control, as evidenced by the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), who does not even know the chief of security or what security costs will be; or the fact that Canadian manufacturers are being deprived of the opportunity to bid for major contracts; and on the fact that over-all costs now seem certain to exceed $1 billion notwithstanding the many direct and indirect federal government commitments.

That the government order an immediate full scale public inquiry into the organization and implementation of the 1976 Olympics in order to reduce any further unnecessary expenditures and so that public confidence in these games can be restored and the games assured of the success Canadians wish them to be.

POSSIBLE INCLUSION OF VICARIOUS LIABILITY SECTION IN GUN CONTROL LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Justice, who has responsibility for introducing changes to the Criminal Code concerning guns. In view of the delay in introducing the legislation, continuing problems in the community and tragedies such as those which occurred at Brampton, Ottawa and other places, will the minister at least inform the public by informing this House if, in the proposed legislation, there is to be included a vicarious liability section under which those who own guns will be responsible for keeping them out of the hands of unstable people or people with a criminal history.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: POSSIBLE INCLUSION OF VICARIOUS LIABILITY SECTION IN GUN CONTROL LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think it is desirable for the Code to be amended in such a way as to create stricter criminal liability. Measures to establish stricter civil liability or to attach civil consequences to the ownership of guns lie largely within the purview of provincial governments and provincial negligence acts. So I answer, first, that I think it desirable to amend the appropriate sections of the Criminal Code in order to increase strict criminal liability for incidents resulting from gun ownership. Also, I think provincial governments should be urged to amend their laws relating to vicarious civil liability along the lines of their motor vehicle acts. These provisions would relate to the owners of guns.

subsubtopic: SWIMMING POOL AT 24 SUSSEX DRIVE
speechtext:
In 1974, after carefully considering the factors, the Prime Minister agreed to accept from a representative group of Canadians the gift of a swimming pool for the official residence at 24 Sussex Drive. In Canada as in most other countries, the making of donations to the state is a common practice and many public buildings have been built as a result of this tradition. The group of donors was concerned that the Prime Minister and his successors have ready access to adequate physical fitness facilities without being confronted with the obvious security and privacy difficulties. The Prime Minister agreed to be one of the contributors. He also chose not to ask for the names of the other contributors, except for their trustee, Dr. W. H. Fader, of 395 Brooks Street, Toronto, lest he be influenced or give the appearance of being influenced by them. The donations, if a properly documented tax return is filed, entitle the contributors to the deductions provided for under Section 110(1 )(b) of the Income Tax Act. Given statutory provisions extant which ensure confidentiality of income tax returns, the government is not in a position to disclose the names of the contributors. The service of Herbert Brune Construction of Ottawa was engaged by the trustee for the donors to install the swimming pool at the official residence. As the costs incurred by that firm have been assumed by private donors, they are not of government record. Since these proposed fitness facilities were to be built on crown-owned land, the Department of Public Works assigned one of its architects to design the pool and related facilities subject to conformity with requirements of the National Capital Commission and the latter's approval at various stages of progress of work. Design costs incurred by the Department of Public Works are the responsibility of the government and are covered by vote 10. As to the operational costs of the facilities, (and related expenditures by departments concerned), they will be included in the overall cost of the administra-

speechtext:

Yes, in the following terms: Question: Mr. Trudeau, in Bonn your visit coincided with the Berlin kidnapping and you told us that the senior German leaders had remarked to you their approval and complimentary views of the way you had handled the Cross and Laporte kidnapping in 1970. Then, in the Chalfont interview the other night, you gave a long account of the democratic principles implicit in your government's actions. subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT

speechtext: The House resumed, from Monday, October 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Andras that Bill C-69, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before I called it ten o'clock last night I was dealing with a number of abuses of the Unemployment Insurance Act and I had categorized them into permissible abuses and those which are not permissible. When I described the case of the fisherman who was embarking upon a holiday trip and loading up his car and his silver trailer, having earned $40,000 that year and having established his status for unemployment insurance benefits for himself and his wife, it was inadvertently recorded in yesterday's Hansard that this particular fisherman came from the city of Prince George. There are no such rich people in Prince George. The fisherman actually came from the city of Prince Rupert, in the riding of my colleague the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo).
During my speech the minister objected to some of the estimates I had placed on the record with regard to the cost to parliament and the country this year of the unemployment insurance fund. I inadvertently mentioned the figure of $2 billion. My notes contained the figure of $1.5 billion, but since my colleague the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) had earlier mentioned the figure of $1.5 billion, and since four hours had expired from the time he spoke until I had the floor, I thought it would be only fair for me to increase the figure a little because costs are going up steadily.
To get back to the people who in my opinion abuse the Unemployment Insurance Act, and speaking about the various segments of our society which use the act for their own purposes, I would like to demonstrate how, in the opinion of the minister, the bill addresses itself to this problem. It proposes to increase the eligibility period from eight weeks to twelve weeks. Rather than reiterate the effect in monetary saving that this would have on the public purse, I will tell the House what this would mean in money and time saved by a person who works in a sausage shop in Victoria. Since she is only suffering from boredom while her husband is away from home, this bill will not have any effect on her. She actually works six to eight months per year, and after that she has an arrangement with her employer to let her go, because her work is usually during the winter months when her employer has problems in obtaining employees.
Also, this bill does not affect fishermen on the west coast with whom I have talked, nor does it affect construction workers whose cases I have described. In the case of fishermen, they have special arrangements with the Unemployment Insurance Commission, and construction workers work longer than the period prescribed in the act. A vast number of Canadians find the services of the Unemployment Insurance Commission convenient when they decide to change jobs frequently just for something to do and without regard to where they will next find employment. The bill addresses itself to that problem as well by extending the waiting period, or disqualification period, from three weeks to six weeks. This means that Canadians who practice frequent job migration will have to wait two months, if clause 16 of the bill is passed, before they qualify for benefits. While this may act as a deterrent to some offenders, it will place unbearable hardship on those people who for just reason, and probably for the first time in their life, leave their employment.
I ask the minister how many Canadians he considers are in a position today to be without income for such a prolonged period of time, particularly in cases where the claimant supports a family. Of all the proposed changes, I find clause 16 the most offensive, for this reason, particularly since there are other ways in which this problem could have been avoided. In most cases people will find it necessary to opt for some form of social assistance in order to bridge the gap. This means, of course-I am sure the minister is aware of this-that the burden of sustaining such a family for the two-month period is shifted partially to the provincial governments.
Before I attempt to suggest solutions to some of the problems I have enumerated-I have done this on previous occasions directly to the minister-I wish to deal with the second category of offenders who benefit from the act illegally. During the last postal strike the minister was surprised to learn that in the Toronto area alone, 6,000 people did not pick up their weekly unemployment insurance cheques at the designated places. One can only speculate that these people had good reason for not presenting themselves to the commission. I am sure some were receiving several weekly payments. Others may have had trouble getting time off from work to collect their cheques. At least that is one positive aspect of a postal strike. Next,

October 28, 1975

there are those who forget to declare earnings from other sources, and those who deliberately make themselves scarce, avoiding offers of employment. The list is seemingly endless, as endless as the army of investigators and adjudicators who roam the regions of our land spying out the guilty but usually only succeeding in punishing the innocent.
I said earlier that the government has not defined for Canadians, or for business or labour in particular, any basic underlying philosophy to the Unemployment Insurance Act. A consultation with business and management, for instance, would reveal that they consider the act to be viewed in the context of insurance only. They have, therefore, considered premiums to be based on a risk factor. The construction workers whom I mentioned would have to pay a higher premium to compensate for their heavy demand on the service.
Labour leaders tell us that they view unemployment insurance as social security and, as such, a redistribution of the general wealth. Based on these predilections, labour is more concerned that all legitimate claims are met and that the system runs at peak proficiency. The total cost is therefore not of concern to labour. Labour would be prepared to trade off the act for some sort of guaranteed income scheme. Little wonder my constituents are confused.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Oh, come on.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
It can be seen that the members of the NDP are also confused. Little wonder that senior citizens, who are now denied access to the benefits of the act, and low income earners who must now pay a higher premium and find their benefit rate reduced, are confused. In light of recent developments, it is surely reasonable to ask the government how much longer it will allow this horrendous disease to go unchecked.
With the implementation of wage and price guidelines, the government has established a precedent which could also apply to the Unemployment Insurance Act. Stern emergency powers are requested by the government to deal with the economic crisis in Canada. The government not only hopes to check but also plans to bring serious budgetary and trade deficits under control. Canadians will be compelled to do certain things and to adhere to certain things. These strong measures became necessary because it was found that restraint did not come voluntarily. Is it not time to insist on similar action with regard to the unemployment situation? After all, it is the single, most contributory factor to the need for deficit financing in our country today.
There are two areas which should be considered immediately. First, we should consider establishing a ceiling of allowable annual earnings beyond which benefits would either not be paid or would have to be refunded with the income tax return. It simply does not make sense to me that a person earning in excess of twice the average Canadian's income should be entitled also to collect UIC benefits for part of the year. Certain professional groups, such as teachers, are already assessed on a 12-month average. Furthermore, serious consideration should be given to restricting the fund to the head of a household in cases
Unemployment Insurance Act
where the combined income of wife and husband exceeds a certain level.
I understand and appreciate the desire of the government to make the program universal and equitable, but the new features in Bill C-69 are anything but that. A significant number of Canadians have reached middle-age and their families have struck out on their own. The husband has reached a peak in his career and enjoys a middle or upper income bracket. The wife, unable to cope with being idle and not having anyone left to care for, opts for some form of employment to keep her busy. She considers it a hobby job, to which she does not wish to become permanently attached. I suspect some of my colleagues in the House of Commons have wives with the same problem who take some kind of job to keep them from becoming bored. My wife does not fit into that category; she does not wish to be a burden on the public purse by accepting any form of income assistance, because she does not need it. I suggest that a number of my colleagues find themselves in the same situation.
It should be our aim to assure a climate of work opportunity in which everyone can find fulfilment; but is it really necessary also to pay benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act during periods when the hobby loses its novelty and it is no longer convenient to go to work? In my case, that is the time I spend in the summer months talking with my constituents in British Columbia.
During our discussion with business and labour it became apparent that due to lack of any kind of demographic profile we were unable to identify these obvious areas of abuse. Also, during our dialogue with business and labour there was no argument when we advanced ideas to consolidate the services of Canada Manpower and the Unemployment Insurance Commission. This brings me to the second area with which the government must concern itself if we ever hope to have a check on UIC spending. It will become imperative to develop a better system of matching jobs with workers.
In a statement to the standing committee on November 26, 1973, the minister stated that the current paradox in Canada, of high unemployment and increasing labour shortages-I am quoting his words- indicates clearly that employers as well as workers may have special problems. I say they do have special problems in Canada. The minister also stated that the heart of any employment service is the technique it uses to match jobs with available workers. He went on to say that in Canada we have used, and used well, the traditional approach to job matching followed by other advanced countries. Nothing, Mr. Speaker, could be further from the truth. The left hand does not know what the right hand is doing. In a survey conducted in my riding we found that Canada Manpower satisfied only 7 per cent to 10 per cent of the available jobs. Only 15 per cent of employers in both the industrial and service sectors consult Manpower at all.
Clearly, Mr. Speaker, what is needed is a complete, and at all times current job inventory. I know these are strong words, but they are not out of season when we talk about some of the other measures the government finally had to bring in. It must be made compulsory for employers to
8618

October 28, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
report their total capacity, and any changes thereto, on a weekly basis. Annual forecasts should also be filed with the commission.
The computer would, as it does in other industrial countries which the minister talked about, compile and reconcile the bank of employment opportunities against those who are looking for work. In that way we would not have to question the honesty and integrity of those who find it necessary to cash in on the unemployment insurance scheme. We would know whether he or she was making himself or herself available for work. We would have information as to the number of jobs available and the types of jobs, and the location would be at the fingertips of the counsellor who dealt with the claim in the first instance. There would be no further need for claim adjudicators and spies to roam around trying to keep everyone honest.
Mr. Speaker, I have advanced these ideas in the form of a private bill to the House and also in a private letter to the minister, pointing out to him the results of my surveys and how other countries cope with the problem. I would like, for the record, to quote a portion of the minister's reply to my submissions. He wrote:
As you may know, enabling legislation exists in the Unemployment Insurance Act to require employers to report job vacancies to my department. This legislation was not repealed after World War II and it remains, as intended, as an instrument to be used in national emergencies.
That is contemporary rhetoric, something we have heard for the last couple of years every time we discuss the economy. He went on:
Measures designed to compel employers to list all job vacancies with the CMC are not compatible, in my opinion, with the current social and economic climate of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I said in my opening remarks that I hope the government will adjust its sails to the prevailing winds in Canada, as they have with the demands Canadians are putting on the economic sea. Bill C-69 fails in this regard. The letter continues:
We are committed to improving departmental services and programs so that employers and workers alike will voluntarily use the CMCs to satisfy their manpower and employment needs.
As I stated to the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee on November 22, 1973, we are now into the first stages of a plan to revitalize the placement service by adopting a more flexible and dynamic approach in the delivery of our services. This approach includes "self-service" job information centres for job ready workers where workers can see up-to-date listings of job vacancies and training opportunities. To date, 18 job information centres have been installed and in these areas placements have increased by 25 per cent. It is planned to introduce these "self-service" JICs in all Canada Manpower Centres across Canada as quickly as possible.
The letter concludes by saying:
All these efforts are directed to giving better service to employers and workers and the experience to date, with the new approach, indicates that we are indeed on the right track.
The letter was written on December 21, 1973. To date, experience indicates that the minister's efforts have been a dismal failure. Mr. Speaker, all of us here know better, of course, and with Bill C-69 the minister admits defeat. He has now decided to shift the burden of costs which he can no longer control to someone else, and he is adjusting his sights as to the rate of unemployment we should aim for in Canada.

It must be a matter of serious concern to us when we see the government's attempts to achieve that by regressive taxation, placing the additional burden on those unfortunate Canadians who can least afford it. It is also a matter of serious concern that we should surrender unconditionally and without a fight to the shortcomings of our economic situation, the improvement of which is the only real solution to the heavy costs in human misery and degradation inherent in unemployment.
Mr. Speaker, as in other fields, this government is failing its people miserably in the area of employment security. The only positive thing the minister suggests in introducing the bill is that in his opinion further changes are absolutely essential. I agree with him on that.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the major argument I have against this bill and the proposed amendments concerns the change in the 4 per cent maximum that the government has used since 1971 as the full employment norm. They changed the ball game completely with regard to economic policy relating to employment policy and the possibility of overcoming unemployment.
This situation has to be viewed against the history of the last 10 or 15 years. In 1965 the Economic Council of Canada made its first report. Dr. Deutsch and his companions defined full employment as an unemployment rate of 3 per cent. Due to the changes in the economy by 1971, the norm was viewed as 4 per cent. With the 1975 budget and the amendments introduced in Bill C-69, the norm is set at an 8 per cent moving average. Actually, nobody can say for sure, now, what the government's full employment norm is. We do know, however, that in June, according to the then minister of finance, it could have been 5.3 per cent and now it would be about 5.7 per cent. It is likely that it will go as high as 6 per cent or 6.5 per cent in the next few years. This is not only reneging on the 1971 white paper but on the definition of the norm of full employment.
I find the government's position interesting. When it introduced its anti-inflation bill, it said that it wanted to see the consumer price index rise by no more than 4 per cent per year in three years. But it refuses to tell us its goals with respect to unemployment. Apparently, according to the bill before us, the government defines full employment as a situation when there is 5.3 per cent unemployment or more.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mostly more.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
The minister and the parliamentary secretary yesterday suggested that as economic conditions have changed so much since 1971, this changed definition as to what constitutes full employment, or the norm in unemployment, is needed. We all know that under this government inflation has reached double-digit levels. We all know that unemployment has risen from an average of some 4.5 per cent in 1970 to an adjusted annual average of 7.2 per cent or 7.3 per cent. This winter, unemployment could easily reach 8 per cent.
It has always been difficult to define what is full employment, and unemployment. Those who represent
October 28, 1975

areas of traditionally high unemployment know that many workers become discouraged and no longer seek jobs. When this happens, when they no longer collect unemployment insurance, they are considered as being out of the labour market and are not counted among the unemployed. As native people are not defined as part of this country's labour force, it is clear that when you talk about 7 per cent or 8 per cent unemployment you are really talking about a total unemployment rate of 10 per cent, 11 per cent or more. The discouraged workers who no longer seek jobs are not included in the labour force survey; they do not count as workers making up the normal part of the labour force in all parts of Canada.
In the 1971 act, the government assumed responsibility for payments when unemployment rose above 4 per cent. Under the present bill, the government will assume responsibility when unemployment rises somewhat above 5 per cent, depending on the eight-year moving average. Clearly the minister, who does not like to be told these things, will make things worse by introducing Bill C-69. The government's response to the present crisis is like the government's ostrich-like response to the housing crisis, a response made evident in the June budget. It is satisfied with glib generalizations and glib cliches like "the changing evolution of our economic realities" which hon. members opposite used yesterday.
The fact is that the unemployed are surplus workers, whether or not they are included in official statistics. The income needs of workers remain the same, even when they are unemployed. It does not matter how bureaucrats define workers as forming part of the official labour force; any unemployed worker has less money to spend. This decreased purchasing power means that we must forgo, in this country, millions of dollars worth of consumption and, therefore, of production. We hear government supporters and members of the official opposition talking about the number of man-days of production lost through strikes, but we never hear them talk of the billions and billions of dollars in goods and services that we could produce if unemployment were kept to within 4 per cent.
We want price stability; we want prices to rise by no more than 4 per cent a year. I cannot understand why we cannot establish a 4 per cent unemployment rate as our goal. But the government has not done this. As I have said, it has done what is politically convenient and it has camouflaged the real situation. Consequently, if we are to get price stability at 4 per cent per year, we might have to settle for an unemployment rate of 7 per cent or 8 per cent as normal. Of course, the minister and his colleagues do not seem to give a darn; they are not on unemployment insurance and most of the middle and high income people they represent are not on unemployment insurance.
The Atlantic provinces and other low income areas of this country will bear the brunt of this legislation. As I see it, our policy-makers are following the lead of Mr. Simon and Arthur Burns in the United States and are content to let unemployment rise to 8 per cent or 9 per cent in order to achieve the goal of prices rising no more than 4 per cent a year. They must know that policies of tight money, high interest rates and fiscal restraint will generate more unemployment. They decided, as is evident from perusal of this bill, to abandon the concept of 4 per cent unemploy-
Unemployment Insurance Act
ment as the norm. They decided to switch the extra burden of the unemployment insurance program to the working poor and other low income groups, worsening the situation of people in low income regions like the Atlantic region.
They did this by introducing a regressive payroll tax, whereas the money ought to be taken from general revenues. In short, this program ought to be based on the progressive income tax concept. The present bill does not say much for present-day liberalism. It is based on basic economic conservatism, a conservatism which is part and parcel of the approach shown by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) to our problems. I have become even more convinced of the truth of this contention since hearing yesterday's interesting exchange between the Minister of Finance and the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees) on the relationship between the money supply and price levels in the economy.
The Minister of Finance struck me as a struggling lawyer trying to understand what the economists, monetarists, bureaucrats and the Bank of Canada are saying, and trying to determine what the whole game is about. The hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings implied in his question that an increased money supply, more than anything, boosts inflation in the short run. The minister seemed to indicate that the Bank of Canada was seriously considering adopting the monetarist point of view and making it part of policy, although he suggested, I understand, that the rules would not be adhered to rigorously as far as economic grant was concerned. I suggest to the Minister of Finance that before he and Governor Bouey become too enamoured of the monetarist view with which Arthur Burns and the federal reserve system of the United States have been toying, they should read the October 20 edition of Business Week, pages 16 and 17. I say this in view of what the minister said yesterday in his exchange with the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings. The editor of Business Week-it is hardly a socialist magazine-stated:
Monetarist economics came into its own back in 1970 when the Fed's open market committee adopted moderate growth of the money supply as a major policy goal. Since then the monetarists, who generally subscribe to Milton Friedman's-
He is a professor at Chicago University, dictum that "inflation is at all times and everywhere a monetary phenomenon," have made numerous converts in the canyons of Wall Street and the executive suites of American business-
Also, I might say, in the Department of Finance and the Bank of Canada.
-so much so that any significant pickup in monetary growth is now taken by many observers as a harbinger of higher inflation.
A newly released study by the prestigious Conference Board, however, suggests that the Fed's preoccupation with gradual monetary growth rests on shaky empirical grounds. In ongoing research reported in the October issue of the Conference Board Record, economist Michael E. Levy employed several equations to explain the inflationary patterns of the past 21 years. Levey found that purely monetarist equations linking short-term monetary growth directly with inflation were the least reliable predictors of subsequent price behaviour.
Therefore, I would advise the Minister of Finance to again get together with Mr. Bouey before making announcements about the latter in effect following the line of Arthur Burns and the federal reserve of the United
29669-62%

October 28, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
States. My conclusion at this point is that this government's policies as envisaged in this bill and the one dealing with anti-inflation will create more unemployment. I also have emphasized that the government has given up the notion of getting back to a 4 per cent level of unemployment in the life of this parliament. They decided then that they had better shift the greater share of the premium-paying for unemployment insurance, since this is bound to go up, to a payroll tax, which falls on the working poor and lower income groups proportionately harder than on middle and upper income taxpayers. We in the Atlantic region, who have so many in the poverty category and the low and middle income groups of this country, will once again be indirectly shafted by the policies of this government which at the same time is protesting they are doing so much through DREE.
I want to discuss for a few minutes the relationship between unemployment insurance and the work ethic, something that was introduced indirectly into this debate yesterday by the minister and picked up by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander). The minister led off this matter with his clause to amend section 43 of the act which refers to disqualification of workers" who leave their jobs without just cause, who refuse suitable employment and who are discharged." He wants the disqualification period changed, raising it from three weeks to six weeks. The proposed changes result from what he called the alarmingly high number of persons leaving their employment. He referred to the annual voluntary quits as being 250,000. I would like to know whether that figure, presumably arrived at after serious study, compared with the ten million people in the labour force, is really alarming. He also seems to think that the figure of 21,000 who annually refuse suitable employment is quite high. It seems to me to be extremely low when you compare 21,000 with a labour force of ten million.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Two hundred and fifty thousand.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
There are 250,000 voluntary quits, and 21,000 who refuse to take suitable employment. The hon. member for Hamilton West dealt more fully with this point in the debate. I want, for his edification and possibly that of the minister-although I shall be more humble in his regard because he has had an opportunity, to do research- through his specialized personnel, to refer to an article by Harold Greer in the Toronto Star this summer, entitled "Matching Jobs and People". This refers to Ontario. I quote:
One of the curious paradoxes of the Canadian labor market in the last few years, especially in this province, has been the phenomenon of high unemployment rates while job opportunities go begging.
It has, of course, been a paradox with highly political implications, in that it invites the conclusion that work is available for anyone who wants it and those who don't are job-dodgers sustained by unemployment insurance benefits. P. E. Trudeau exploited that idea very adroitly in the last federal election campaign, even as he cracked down on claimants for the expanded benefits introduced by his government in 1971.
It is not, however, a conclusion supported by a research study by the Ontario ministry of labor. In a paper entitled "The Paradox of Unemployment and Job Vacancies-Some Theories Confronted by Data," M. L. Skolnik and F. Siddiqui of the ministry's research branch find little evidence for, and much against, the theory that laziness and unemployment insurance explain the coexistence of unemployment and manpower shortages.
Going away from Ontario to those parts of the country where you would expect the most abuses because unemployment has been around so long, I want to refer to discussion paper No. 33 of a study by the Economic Council of Canada for the Council of Maritime Premiers last year. In that document, which studied the relationship of unemployment insurance to labour market activities, among other areas, there is a chapter entitled "The Effect of the Unemployment Insurance System" of 1971 and the increased benefits of labour force activity in the Atlantic region. I will just use a short quote from the conclusion of the chapter:
The greater generosity of the unemployment insurance system has not decreased true labour force participation in the maritimes.
In other words, rather than the bias of those who are trying constantly to say there are too many people using unemployment insurance in the Atlantic region, this study strongly suggests that if the jobs are there, the people will take the jobs. They want the jobs. Of course, this flies in the face of those who say there is a disappearing work ethic as far as Canada is concerned, even in parts of Canada where there is heavy unemployment constantly, as in the Atlantic region.
One of the amendments the minister suggested yesterday which seems eminently fair is that which extends the choice of weeks for a pregnant employee. An amendment I should like the House to consider arises out of an experience we had, admittedly in an emergency situation, in my constituency this summer. Perhaps I can best introduce it by reading part of a letter from Mr. Daniel White, vicepresident of local 4520 of the United Mine Workers of America, district 26, after a fire in the only coal mine in Glace Bay had resulted in the loss of 775 jobs and pushed unemployment as recorded in the Glace Bay unemployment insurance office up to between 26 and 29 per cent. Mr. White wrote:
The membership of No. 26 local union 4520 are requesting the assistance of your office in helping us to determine whether we have been unjustly treated under the UIC Act with regard to the disqualification of a week's waiting period which followed the fire at No. 26 colliery on June 19, 1975.
The week following this date the men had no work and were putting in a week's waiting period under the UIC Act. However, retroactive money due to the men dating back to January 1, 1975, was paid to the miners on the Thursday of that week. According to the UIC Act this disqualified the men from a week's waiting period. The membership feel this was an abnormal situation and this retroactive pay was issued early due to the unforeseen circumstances.
The background to this is that the last contract negotiated between the United Mine Workers and the Cape Breton Development Corporation included a clause giving the miners benefits in case of lay-offs. The terms of the agreement provided for $100 for the first week and $20 a day for the second week, up to a maximum of $200. This was certainly a step forward and both the mine union and DEVCO should be commended for it. It was put in to help the men get by their two-week waiting period for UIC benefits. Unfortunately, the unemployment insurance regulations under section 172, "determination of earnings for benefit purposes", section 1 and 2(a), defeat the purpose of this arrangement by treating the payment as "income of a claimant arising out of any employment".

October 28, 1975

As the act now stands, this $200 payment would have penalized the miners in the eyes of the UIC if it had been paid during the first two weeks. To prevent this happening, DEVCO, in conjunction with the union, worked out a plan under which the unemployed men would be paid a special advance at the rate of $15 per week. Under the circumstances, this was the best way of giving the miners the money due to them, with the least penalization.
The upshot was that the $30 for the first two weeks was deducted from the first UIC payment on the third week. This is because any money received during the two-week waiting period is deducted from the claimant's first UIC cheque. The balance of the $15 payments to the claimants by DEVCO did not affect UIC payments because such a sum is below the minimum allowable earnings received while collecting UIC. To give an example, a miner eligible for $100 in UIC benefits would have received $15 from DEVCO in the first week, $15 from DEVCO in the second week, and $70 from UIC in the third week along with DEVCO'S $15. In the fourth week he would have received the full $100 from UIC, plus $15 from DEVCO. The additional payment of $15 from Devco would have continued until the miner had received a total of $200.
Mr. Speaker, the miners effectively lost $30 of their benefit because it was deducted from their first UIC cheque. This is regrettable. But far more disturbing, in the eyes of the miners, is that they cannot collect this special payment during the first two weeks when they need it most. Admittedly, a fire in the mine-which is what caused these lay-offs-is an emergency which does not occur every day, but things like this ought to be provided for under appropriate regulations of the UIC. It is intolerable that UIC regulations should conspire against a good agreement worked out between management and union to help the unemployed miner.
The regulations should be changed so as to allow DEVCO miners and other workers with similar agreements to draw special payments during the waiting period without being penalized. In such urgent cases, the waiting period should be drastically cut or eliminated completely. There is also a need to clarify whether or not forgiveable loans from the company in times of hardship or emergency should really be computed as earnings by the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
I want to conclude by saying that the amendments embodied in Bill C-69, especially the regressive tax elements in it as well as the change of the 4 per cent norm, lead us to realize that over on the other side is not a government of compassionate liberalism but a government of confusion in objectives and means to obtain its objectives, with more than a little bias against low income workers and low income regions. This is all underscored in the government's anti-inflation program and the changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act which the minister introduced yesterday.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill presented in the House on July 20, 1975 includes amendments meant more particularly to protect the fund than the worker confronted with the unemploy-
Unemployment Insurance Act
ment problem, a social evil hitting too many well disposed persons. As a result many problems crop up and often lead to poverty with its usual consequences.
It is proper to examine for a moment the situation of an individual tackling with the unemployment problem. The head of the family who loses his job feels that it is the end of everything. He cannot bear facing his wife, his children and his friends. If he does find temporary employment it will usually be a semi-skilled job with low wages. He is deprived of the necessaries of life and he is also suffering from psychological deprivation. He got a better salary in his previous job and was proud of his work, whereas he feels humiliated in his new position. He feels rejected, his pride withers.
When the head of the family is at home all day long and has to face financial troubles and feels sorry and helpless, he sometimes becomes irritable and difficult to put up with, and his family life suffers as a consequence. He feels sorry for himself and guilty at the same time. His situation gets even worse when he sees prosperity around him. After six months or maybe a little more, his standard of living deteriorates and he becomes one of the unprivileged. If he has completed only primary or secondary studies, is unskilled and over 45, he has but little hope to find a satisfactory job and his chances get smaller and smaller every day.
Let me by the way mention that aspect of unemployment which I call dangerous. It can become explosive if handled by opportunists, mind you. In these days of hardship, the executives and personnel of news media, the employees of the Unemployment Insurance Commission and manpower centres should perform their task in a totally unbiassed way, and be careful not to let themselves be prompted into a provoking answer which might increase existing social tensions. We, in this Parliament, should use every parliamentary procedure to have the government start with all the means at its disposal looking for real solutions to the great problems of today. We should provide the civil servants who assume responsibility for enforcing the bills we pass with the appropriate means to really help the unemployed who show their good will. They have been hit by a hard enough blow when they left their employment. Let them not be submitted to endless vexations before they can be paid benefits.
When referring to the July 8 memo, I find that the amendments in Bill C-69, which are important in some ways, are mainly changes aimed at smoothing out some of the drawbacks inherent in the enforcement of the act. I notice in the documentory notes given to us on July 8 a reference to a number of supplementary changes proposed to reduce as much as possible the injustices and complexities now existing. I notice this reference and I hope that fuller changes will be introduced without too much delay.
As regards persons who take part in job creation projects, such as local initiatives program promoters, it is normal that they take part in the benefits as well as inconveniences deriving from the Unemployment Insurance Act. The proposed changes also mention that claimants may be allowed to terminate a current benefit period and establish a new one, if it is in their interest to do so.
This procedure might be profitable, especially in the case of payments for an illness, since there is always the

October 28, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
question of an initial phase. About this kind of benefits, changes are also suggested to ease somewhat the eligibility conditions. The problem of medical certificates will have to be settled, and the certificates provided by local physicians will have to be deemed as valid for eligibility purposes without any need for confirmation by other physicians at the head office of the commission who do not know anything of the patient's illness.
I have here a photocopy of a letter adressed to a claimant who had incurred an illness during the initial period. I think it is appropriate to quote from it a paragraph which shows the difficulties which result from the act and the related regulations. It reads:
The claimant submitted a second application for the week of December 22, 1974. She provided us with an employment record with eight weeks of insurable employment between December 9, 1973 and February 2, 1974. However, she needed 8 weeks between December 23, 1973 and December 28, 1974, which was her reference period, that is to say 52 weeks from the date of her second application.
This is a real mathematical problem and the result is a big zero for total payment. Insurable period, initial period, reference period are so many words used by officials to try explain the periods when there is no payment at all.
I have often said in the House that the Unemployment Insurance Act, while providing a necessary help to unemployed people, is also set up first of all to protect the fund. We see clearly an example of such a financial cooperation in this provision regarding the benefit disentitlement after the age of 65, since the former Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) himself announced this feature in his budget speech last June 23. We cannot be blind to the fact that those workers have contributed to the unemployment insurance scheme for many years, in the hope of keeping their entitlement to benefits till the age of 70. It is an injustice for this group of workers, and we do not think the savings permitted by this measure will contribute significantly to balance the budget.
Most of those workers re poor people who would deserve better treatment at an age when they are still available and eager to do some work according to their skill. Representations have already been made by representatives of various associations on behalf of their group, and it would be advisable that this discretionary measure be completely deleted from the bill under study.
If the technocrats who drafted Bill C-69 had really been concerned about the workers, they would have found, at the very least, a solution to the transfer of the contributions, either to the Quebec Pension Plan or the Canada Pension Plan, in order to increase appreciably the inome of the workers in the event where they were forced into retirement. It is inconceivable that workers who for years have contributed to maintain an insurance fund should be faced with the denial of their right to benefits when they are still available on the labour market, and without compensation from a fund to which they have contributed for many a year.
I therefore urge the minister to at least find a solution that is more humane.
On September 22, 1975, the Quebec newspaper Le Soleil reported that the delegates of the golden age at the close of
the convention of the federation attended by delegates of 802 affiliated clubs, representing 90,000 members of the federation, expressed the wish that their federation exert pressures on the government to convince it of withdrawing Bill C-69 through which persons over 65 will be denied the right to unemployment insurance benefits.
On September 5, 1975, the secretary of the Quebec Retired Civil Servants Association Incorporated sent the members of parliament and the news media copy of the resolution passed at a meeting of the administrative council of the association convened on September 2, 1975.
Here are some extracts of the whereases in their resolution:
That the proposed amendment is unfair and discriminatory for those who are 65 or more and who, because they do not have sufficient income to live comfortably in these inflation times, have a job and hope to be able to get unemployment insurance benefits in a more or less distant future after they have contributed to the fund for many years.
That the government established a program called "New Horizons" aimed at keeping active those who are 65 or more by encouraging them to have a job to stay in good health as long as possible.
That the government spent in this regard $10 million and that a sound and fair philosophy ensures that those who take part in this program are not penalized, as would be the case if the bill were enacted.
That the Minister of Manpower and Immigration is drafting legislation to make courses available to the unemployed so that they can have a new training to get a job, thus integrating manpower training programs into the unemployment insurance program.
That a pilot project is now on trial in Newfoundland, under which a larger number of unemployed would receive both unemployment insurance benefits and some training, which would create, if the experience were successful, a glaring contradiction with the provisions of Bill C-69.
It is therefore proposed and resolved unanimously that the government of Canada be urged to delete in this bill all provisions relating to the non-eligibility for unemployment insurance benefits of people aged 65 or more, in order that the latter, as in the past, be entitled to eventually receive total benefits after termination of employment.
I have in hand the text of a communique appearing in Le Droit of Ottawa on Friday, September 19, 1975, signed by Mrs. Wilbrod Dufour, from Sainte-Foy and entitled: "The hell with people aged 65 or more". It is a good opportunity during this debate to quote the whole text of that communique, which summarizes so well the situation:
This title may seem a little startling but in my view it faithfully reflects the federal government's attitude towards older workers. Indeed we read in the budget speech that the applicants' age limit will be lowered from 70 to 65.
What is the rationale? To keep afloat the unemployment insurance fund which is supposed to be in the red. If the unemployment insurance is poorly administered, one cannot blame it on the older workers.
I support this statement 100 per cent.
What is meant by "older worker"? It is someone who has reached or will shortly reach the age of 65. He is about to be dismissed from his job because he has reached the compulsory retirement age which is

October 28, 1975	COMMONS DEBATES_________________________________________ 8623
enforced in the business where he is employed. He may be entitled to a meagre pension or he may not. And surely the old age pension cannot fill the grap and provide him with decent livelihood. Therefore he has to work.
Many of these people enjoy good health and are perfectly capable of working. They are bona fide workers as defined in the Unemployment Insurance Act. It is precisely because they make many contacts to find a job that they need unemployment benefits. Nevertheless the government has just arbitrarily decided that at 65 a man has no right to work, in a word no right to live. Yet most of them have contributed to the unemployment insurance fund for 34 years-since 1941-and in many instances have never collected benefits.
This important group of people, made up of elderly workers and their families, is compelled to judge very harshly the governing body for wanting to treat them in such a way.
Is there anything more enlightening than to hear our federal ministers utter, on every possible occasion, pious wishes with regard to our senior citizens: they built our society, they deserve our respect, our regards, our consideration, etc.
But when it is time for action they merely think of getting the Unemployment Insurance Fund out of the red at the expense of the elderly workers, those who built it by contributing to it for 34 years.
It is obvious that all those who contributed for many years to the Unemployment Insurance Fund deserve a lot of attention from the administration. They are not responsible for the administrative complexities resulting from a legislation and regulations that should be improved on the basis of the needs of everyone of its participants.
Most of these workers are poor people who should deserve a better treatment at an age where they are still available and ready to work within their capabilities. We do not believe that the savings resulting from this measure will be useful in balancing the budget.
I am convinced that this measure will not help balance the budget. However, it can easily be seen that a legislation with a too sophisticated phraseology brings out regulations which often are inapplicable. Insurability problems could be eliminated to a degree with some appropriate amendment to the multiplication of the waiting and qualifying period, the extended period and the length of the employment period and to the total earnings with the same employer.
The four consecutive weeks of ineligibility, although it might be due to four weeks of work, is a feature which has to come out of the Unemployment Insurance Act. It contributes to discourage the unemployed to go back to work.
Recently, in my riding the employees of the Moto-ski plant had been called back to work by their employer for a four week period and when they re-established their claim they lost in its entirety the unemployment insurance to which they were legitimately entitled simply because of the formulation of a section of the act that did not mean anything.
These difficulties arising out of a poorly written act might sometimes lead to illogical decisions on the part of an officialdom qost in that complexe red tape.
I shall give you an example of what happened when eligibility to pregnancy benefit had to be determined. Here is the answer given by an employee of the Commission to a claimant: That claimant does not meet the eligibility requirements for pregnancy benefits. She does not have, as mentioned in the regulation, the 10 insurable employment weeks during the 20 week period immediately preceding the thirtieth week before her delivery. During
Unemployment Insurance Act
this period, she made no contribution and, as a result, she received no payments. Can you imagine such administrative complications?
As concerns job searching, it is sometimes revolting to see what happens. Unemployed workers are required to visit employers who are having extreme difficulty remaining in operation in an industry like the furniture industry, because of higher transport rates between provinces, like the leather goods industry which must bear the fluctuations of custom rates, like the wood industry in general which is half paralysed. The type of cooperation which must exist between manpower employees and Unemployment Insurance Commission employees should help the unemployed instead of giving them trouble.
To give an idea of the answers given concerning job searching, I would like to read question No. 2095 placed on the order paper on March 21, 1975, at the request of my colleague from Abitibi. It is as follows:
Question: Does the Unemployment Insurance Commission have daily data on the number and type of jobs available in a region and, if so, how does the Commission inform the concerned citizen?
Answer: Yes but these data are maintained by district office rather than region to enable the Commission's local offices to provide a more effective service to UIC claimants as distinct from the concerned citizen at large. This information is used for adjudication purposes and to assist claimants in meeting their obligation to seek and find work.
That gives an idea of the problem caused by the regulations concerning job searching. It is obvious that the commission has required the unemployed to search for more jobs than there can possibly be available at certain times of the year. It must be noted that the cost of advisory services in job reference or research is evaluated at $1,345,730 for Canada and at $427 million for Quebec.
I believe that these sums would have been better used if more projects had been accepted through the Local Initiatives or the Opportunities for Youth Programs. All the preparation work had required different types of research and this was not costing the government a penny, and the projects in most cases were valid ones. This would have provided work for many unemployed anxious to work. The same thing will happen again there.
In my area 82 projects were submitted. We have $1,077,000 to distribute and there are projects for over $3 million. So imagine that some will have to be told that their projects are not accepted. And the unemployment rate in our area varies from 17 to 25 per cent based on the calculations usually used by the officials of various boards under the Department of Labour. I have never been against the idea of implementing the Local Initiative Program, it was fantastic, it required preparation work on the part of people. The spirit of initiative was being discovered in workers, well-intentioned people. But at the same time provision should have been made for sufficient amounts to accept at least two thirds of the projects. We cannot accept more than one third.
This year some advertising was done to encourage people to submit projects. Yes, there is a lot of unemployment. A lot of money was paid to advertise and then discourage people because most projects are not accepted. That was a way of solving the unemployment. That avoided the red tape complications of an overly complicated legislation.

October 28, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
The consideration of a bill whose object is to reduce the demoralizing effects of inflation should not take us away from another objective whose purpose would be to take the appropriate means to organize work so more citizens can participate each according to his tastes, skills, aspirations and knowledge. There is so much work to do in a young country like ours.
I would not suggest there is nothing good in Bill C-69. Only I wanted to show the act's deficiencies in general, as I had reasons to believe more sections would be amended. However, I recognize extending the eligibility period will help some unemployed persons. Those that suffer from an accident will receive certain benefits. But I note these various clauses are still couched in a way that makes them very complicated and difficult to understand by the majority of unemployed workers. It is hoped the bill will be amended, either in committee or elsewhere, to become acceptable.
I still feel officials from the department and the UIC do not adequately consult labour representatives before they prepare this kind of legislation. For this reason, and unduly large proportion of unemployed are victimized under the act, which does not relate to present day needs.
Extending the disqualification period for those who leave their jobs without good reason or refuse suitable employment may have serious repercussions. I do not approve of a worker leaving his job without a good reason or refusing suitable employment. However, we should consider the circumstances and the kind of employment offered. This is where arbitrary decisions will happen.
It may be said that the unemployed can always appeal, but that is a long and complicated process. We should certainly add something that would force the officials to scrutinize the case before they render a decision. I do not criticize the officials as a whole, because most of them are relatively well inclined. However, let us make it easier for them. The legislation is so complicated they are sometimes compelled to take attitudes contrary to common sense. According to my information, the commission employs 118 investigators for the province of Quebec and 26 liaison officers. By comparing the number of investigators and liaison officers, one can conclude that the commission is taking more interest in investigations than on information given to claimants about their entitlements and liabilities.
On several occasions, I mentioned that complications have multiplied when the commission appealed to the income tax office to determine the insurability, this fact has caused many a headache. And if that continues, no one knows when it will end. I have in hand an advertisement published in newspapers indicating the computing methods to use for reimbursing to the Department of National Revenue the overpayments of unemployment benefits. A whole page, 8V2 by 14 inches, just to explain how to pay back the overpayments. A fine example of cooperation, indeed, which does more for the unemployment insurance funds than for the interests of the unemployed. We seldom see the commission advertise to explain to the unemployed how to get an adjustment of their benefits in case of miscalculations. No wonder the Unemployment Insurance Act is the target of so many criticisms. I attempted to explain that it is mainly because it is often written in quite an incomprehensible manner.

I have here an editorial by CJRC dated October 10, 1975 and entitled "The Unemployment Insurance Scandal". I would like to quote in part. It reads as follows:
It is an open secret that thousands of unemployed draw unemployment insurance benefits to which they are not entitled, through the help or the ignorance of some UIC officials, while thousands of others who would be entitled to those benefits have seen the payment of benefits being refused, through arbritrary action of officials, both intransigent and arrogant!
And one reads further down:
Let me quote now the content of a memorandum adressed to UIC officials by insurance director D. R. Brown, which, however unlikely it may seem, reads as follows:
"It is not the responsibility of commission officials to inform the parties concerned that the time may have come for them to submit a claim for benefits, nor to invite them to submit one, NOR TO KEEP THEM INFORMED OF THEIR POSSIBLE BENEFIT ENTITLEMENT.
The insured who claims that he or she did now know the provisions of the act, nor his or her resulting duties and obligations HAS NO ADMISSIBLE EXCUSE IN CASE OF NEGLIGENCE". This confidential document has fallen into our hands; it is reproduced in its integrity for your information. You will certainly ask yourselves, as we do, if the unemployment insurance scheme is not a poor joke, and if the UIC is not mocking benefit recipients who are at its mercy.
I should like to conclude by insisting on the employment search problem. For some time and especially since last fall, commission officials have certainly given instructions to their employees as to the recipient's obligation to search for employment. I am not against commission employees suggesting the unemployed ways and means to find employment. Let's not go too far however. Various factors must be taken into account with regard to job seeking. First the unemployment rate in the area, the number of industries likely to need manpower; the season in the case of forestry, farm, fisheries workers or of any other seasonal industry; besides, and this is very important, the working and wage conditions that prevail in the area where the worker is sent; travelling expenses, the approximate duration of the job and that must be checked by people well informed of the prevailing working conditions in the area suggested to the unemployed.
It is well known that those directives resulted in forcing unemployed to seek jobs in areas where manpower centre employees had no job to offer. Those bureaucratic requirements do not solve the unemployment problem, but rather help wear out the patience, and I repeat it, the patience of overstaffed employers and of unemployed who lose heart when they see the results of their efforts.
I conclude by expressing the hope that the bill will nonetheless be revised, re-examined and, after consideration in committee, practical suggestions will be made and most of all studied by those in power so there will be major amendments to improve a little the sometimes complex relations that result from a legislation drafted in a way that is not suitable to those who are out of work.

speechtext:
The applause must mean that they would like me to finish as quickly as possible.
There was one sentence, particularly, in the speech the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) made to the House yesterday which caught my attention and which, it appears from Hansard, received considerable commendation in the House. That sentence is as follows:
-we intend to make certain that Canadians who are working hard to maintain self-sufficiency, to maintain the momentum of this country's economy, and who are contributing to the unemployment insurance program, do not have to carry the added burden of supporting ablebodied people who do not want to work.
That is an indication by the minister that he is concerned about the problem colloquially called a rip-off but perhaps more accurately called abuses which attach not only to the Unemployment Insurance Commission but to many progams both inside and outside government. There are problems of cheaters and chisellers in relation to avoiding Customs, as we all know. There was even cheating and chiselling with regard to the guaranteed income supplement, though we do not talk about that very much. These cheaters and chisellers are a small proportion of those who might benefit from any program.
If I understood the remarks of the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan) earlier, he suggested that perhaps the number was not terribly significant and that we should not worry overly about this kind of abuse of the program. I suppose it would be easy to reply that as long as any abuse is taking place, members of parliament should be concerned with saving taxpayers money. However, even more important, I think it would be fair to suggest that it is important that the unemployment insurance program should have the credibility which requires those who abuse the system to be cut to the absolute minimum and that the cheaters and chisellers be sought after and, hopefully, caught. It is not simply a question of absolute numbers. It is a question that the program must not only be just but it must appear to the public to be one in which the interest of the public is protected through efficiency and through concern about those who might abuse the system.
Where I would agree with the hon. member is that we should not, in that tired old phrase, throw out the baby with the bath water. In concerning ourselves with abuses and the necessity of restricting them, we must make sure not to limit the benefits under the program for those who are genuinely deserving of them. In bureaucratic jargon, concern about abuses is translated into the phrase "the disincentive to work problem." That is a phenomenon we have had to deal with in terms of unemployment insurance since the inauguration of the scheme in 1941.
There is a continuing dilemma with regard to this program. On one hand, benefits under the system must be adequate in order to meet the primary objective of offering adequate income replacement to those who are unemployed, but in so doing we must keep in mind the disincentive to work. If these benefits are too high, they may cause people to try to take advantage of them when they are not entitled to do so.
Unemployment Insurance Act
One way of dealing with the problem of disincentive to work would be to ensure that the benefits under the program were so small that people would not have an incentive to leave work and accept the benefits. That would certainly minimize the problem. If benefits were reduced to an extremely low level-I am sure no one in this House would like to see that happen-individuals would be forced back into the labour market and obliged to take any kind of work because of the inadequacy of the benefits under the program.
However, the effect of taking the action of reducing benefits would be dramatic in its influence on Canada's labour force and on the economy. It is desirable for highly skilled people to retain their skills, but they would be forced to accept less skilled, or unskilled jobs in order to survive. The social investment and their investment in their training and education, and the effect of their education would be lost to the labour market.
Clearly, the effects of the disincentive to work in any unemployment insurance scheme must be weighed carefully against the need to maintain the stability of the labour market, to protect skills and to maintain a pool of trained workers from which the economy can draw in times of high productivity. Many employers are forced to have periods of lay-off. They need, and it is desirable, to have their work force readily available when production resumes. It would be costly and damaging if the work force of those employers was unavailable because of inadequate unemployment insurance protection which would force them to disperse what would otherwise be a skilled work force.
Clearly, what we must do is try and draw a balance in dealing with the disincentive to work problem between the needs of maintaining high levels to protect those who are legitimately without work and to find, also, mechanisms which will discourage those who might be tempted to cheat on the system, who might be tempted to try to find ways of claiming benefits when they are not genuinely those which the act has in mind as beneficiaries.
I was pleased to see that the minister, in bringing forth this legislation-though he did not deal with this in great length in his speech to the House-has taken steps to deter individuals from unfairly battening on to the system. The most significant of these changes is the proposal that those who voluntarily quit their jobs without good cause, those who are discharged for misconduct, those who refuse suitable employment, and those who refuse to upgrade their skills by taking courses of instruction, will be disqualified from receiving benefits up to a maximum of six weeks.
This is not simply an extension of the maximum; it is, in effect, a doubling of the penalties under the existing act. Those under the existing act who were penalized by one week's disqualification would now face two weeks disqualification, those with two weeks would face four, and those with three would face six. It is perhaps misleading to say that it is an extension of the maximum disqualification; it is, in effect, a doubling of the disqualification under the existing act.
Under the old Unemployment Insurance Act, the disqualification was simply a deferment of benefits, not a

October 28, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
reduction in the number of weeks payable. The Gill committee, which studied the Unemployment Insurance Act more than ten years ago, recommended that the penalty be a loss in benefits rather than a deferment, and that provision was introduced in 1971. With the current proposal, people who quit their job without good cause face up to eight weeks, including the two-week waiting period, without benefits. I hope this will be a disincentive to those who might be tempted to take advantage of the system.
I know there are some members on the other side of the House, and perhaps even on this side, who consider six weeks disqualification to be harsh. There will be some who under some circumstances-and I might put myself in this category-feel that it is not harsh enough. There are jurisdictions in which those who leave employment voluntarily or are discharged for misconduct, and so on, lose all entitlement to benefit and must requalify through working in insurable employment.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman across the way is knowledgeable of activities in Spain, but one can look closer than that, to the United States, and see that they have that kind of provision.
The government has decided that approach would be unduly harsh, and feel that the provision they have brought forward meets the middle ground. It is a more desirable disqualification, and more generous than the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) would like to see followed. I hope it will have the effect of retarding unjustified demands on the system which we, as representatives of the taxpayers, should be concerned about.
The second provision in the legislation which I support relates to the three weeks' lump sum advance payment of benefits to claimants, which does not have to be repaid in the event that they find work immediately. This was introduced in the 1971 act and we on this side supported it because it was felt that we were adding an incentive to those who were unemployed to get back to the work force quickly. It was conceived as an incentive to re-enter the work force. It was assumed that this kind of lump payment would be a bonus on top of the salary an individual would receive, and so he would be extra active in efforts to find work quickly.
Unfortunately, the opposite proved to be the case. Rather than being an incentive to early return to work, advance payments of unemployment insurance in many cases seems to have resulted in a disincentive. There appears to be evidence that those receiving the payment did not return to the work force more quickly than other people. It appears that the 1971 legislation conferred incentives and benefits which did not have the intended effect, so it seems logical to discontinue them.
In summary, Madam Speaker, one of the reasons I am anxious to support this legislation is that it takes steps to reduce the disincentive to work which, perhaps unfairly, in the public mind has been associated with the unemployment insurance program. These are useful steps to diminish the kind of cheating that could take place, and I think they will assure the public that we are concerned about that problem.

I hope the minister will not be complacent in the administration of this legislation. In the last three years I know there have been considerable improvements in the consideration of the act and improved liaison between the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the Canada Manpower division of the Department of Manpower and Immigration. There are now better procedures, however, to ensure that persons receiving unemployment insurance benefits are made aware of and are given the option of suitable job opportunities as early as possible. The commission has developed an active job search program. This means that persons in receipt of benefits must prove they are making reasonable and customary efforts to find jobs during the time they are receiving the benefits.
There have been improvements in the administration of the program, but I do not believe the minister should be sanguine or content or overly satisfied with the administrative application of this program. My concern is not for the basis of the program, which I support entirely. My concern is that since such a large proportion of public funds is involved, the program should be operated with the utmost efficiency. Those who are not entitled to benefits under the program should not receive them: public support for the program will thus be maintained.
I think it is a necessary program and we must maintain its credibility. That can be done through effective enforcement of the present procedures and the steps the minister has shown he is prepared to take to dissuade those who might feel they can get away with ripping off such a program.
