speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have listened with keen interest to the debate thus far. While it is obvious that there are some problems with the suggested amendments, as referred to by many members, particularly from this side of the House, I should like to address myself to the few points relating to some amendments which should have been included in the bill but for some reason were not.
I refer to the inequities which have always existed in the Unemployment Insurance Act as related to fishermen. To me, it is entirely inexcusable that after so very many promises made over the past few years to bring in an income support program for fishermen, there is still no sign of anything realistic happening in this area. Until the government comes up with that type of income support program, interim amendments should be introduced to satisfy the needs of the fishermen and to overcome the inequities and discrimination which exist in the present act. The only reference to fishermen that I have found is contained in the information papers on Bill C-69, issued by the minister, dealing with the exclusion of fishermen from the general rule of employer-employee relationships. Unfortunately, this is always the case and is always referred to.
If I may digress for a moment, Madam Speaker, I wonder why a clear definition cannot be made between a fisherman employer and an employee. When is a fisherman going to get equal consideration with others in the work force? It is true that a fisherman who owns a lon-gliner and his sharemen can be considered as selfemployed, but in the general rule the act is discriminatory toward those who contribute. If the department respon-
October 28, 1975

sible, and the Department of National Revenue, consider fishermen eligible to pay premiums, then surely they should be entitled to equal benefits.
Many suggestions have been made along the following lines from interested parties in all areas of the country: One is that fishermen would be eligible on the same basis as at present, that is, with eight weekly contributions. However, eight contributions entitle fishermen to benefits for 12 weeks. Each additional week of contributions should entitle a fisherman to IV2 weeks of benefits, to a maximum of 24 weeks. The period of eligibility should be extended by two months. This would give the fishermen greater flexibility in determining when they would draw benefits, and would be more realistic in view of the fact that the normal fishing season varies in different parts of the country, particularly in the province of Newfoundland. The amount of benefits should be calculated by averaging all weekly contributions, and trawler fishermen should be placed on the same basis as regular employees. At the present time, claims may be established between the week in which December 1 falls and the week in which May 15 falls, and the benefit period runs from the week in which the claim is established to the week in which May 15 next falls, unless benefits are exhausted at an earlier date.
We have been told time and time again that an income support program will be forthcoming. This process even went to the extent that early in 1974 the previous minister of the environment, the Hon. Jack Davis, wrote to provincial ministers asking for their views on the contemplated income support program. In their reply, the Newfoundland government urged the implementation of the program to be no later than the start of the fishing season in 1975, and requested that they be involved in formulating the administrative and implementation details.
The province recommended that in the event of a delay certain changes should be introduced in the intervening period. Further, they suggested modifications which were compatible with the proposed income support program and their adoption of it. They suggested that this would ease the transition from the unemployment insurance program to the income support scheme, as follows. The effect of adopting their suggestions would be to increase the flexibility of the defined employment and benefit periods. They stated that current definitions are too rigid and preclude consideration of the variability of local fishing seasons. It was suggested that the beginning and end of the fishing season should be determined each year and for each geographic zone on the basis of weather and ice conditions in each zone. The length of the fishing season could be determined jointly with the federal Department of Fisheries after consultation with local fishermen, union officials and members of the industry. The method for determining the number of benefit weeks should be the same for fishermen as for regular claimants. The rule that the total number of benefit weeks cannot exceed five-sixths of the insured employment period should therefore be eliminated. The only limitation should be this, that no benefits may be paid to any fishermen in any zone during the defined fishing season in that zone.
I suggest that the limit of $170 per week on a fisherman's maximum insured earnings should also be eliminat-
Unemployment Insurance Act
ed. Currently, maximum insurable earnings are determined on a weekly and annual basis. I think the figure used for an annual basis is $8,840. Fishing income is highly variable, and if a fisherman is lucky he can earn $2,000 in a couple of weeks. But only $340 of the sum earned in two weeks is counted as insurable earnings. This inequity, under which the extra amount earned is excluded, should be corrected because the fisherman might earn no more for the rest of the year. That amount may represent his total earnings for the year.
So, here we are, almost at the end of 1975, still lacking income support legislation. The minister indicated that legislation would soon be introduced to provide for an income support program. I only hope that this will happen. If it does not, I suggest that it is incumbent on the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras), who is responsible for unemployment insurance matters, to amend Bill C-69 in the way I have suggested. There is still opportunity for him to introduce such amendments.
The other point I want to make concerns discrimination against women in the fishing industry. In this regard, it is obvious that those responsible for the equality of status of women have completely missed evidence of discrimination against women who are or can be employed in the fishing industry. The Unemployment Insurance Act discriminates in its provision for benefits. Why do I say that? At certain times of the year, certain species of fish are in abundance. Then, manpower on an emergency basis is needed to process certain delicate species such as scallops.
To illustrate the disparity, let me refer to an incident which took place in a remote area of Newfoundland. In order to process the scallops, manpower is needed. Naturally, the people of the area found it impossible to contact a Manpower centre 200 or 300 miles away in order to apply for personnel for processing the scallops. Therefore, it naturally fell on the fishermen to hire their families and wives. Before doing so, they checked with the Department of National Revenue and were told by an official that they could not hire their wives. A fisherman could only hire his neighbour's wife. In turn, that neighbour could hire the fisherman's own wife. The people of the area accepted this decision made by a responsible official, but the decision was overruled by superiors. The result was overpayments of UIC benefits to many individuals, to say nothing of the resulting embarrassment and financial difficulties.
This situation has continued for almost two years and stems from ridiculous regulations which neither the UIC nor the Department of National Revenue can reconcile, despite their supposed expertise. As I say, no attempt has been made to clarify this predicament or to correct the regulations. Neither was any reference made to this inequity in Bill C-16. I suggest that an amendment to Bill C-16 could have corrected the situation. I only hope that the ministers responsible will address themselves to this serious discrepancy and I hope the government will act to wipe out overpayments made to the innocent victims concerned.
May I comment on the bill itself, Madam Speaker? I think the minister should be taking a harder look at the uniformity with which the regulations are applied, particularly in view of varying conditions existing in different regions of the country, conditions to do with the

October 28, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
geographic, economic and social situation of the area concerned. Certainly, the number of grievances with which members of parliament are daily inundated should indicate that something is wrong with the system. For example, I ask the minister to refer to section 39 of the act, which authorizes the commission to refer claimants to approved courses of instruction and to waive the requirement for the claimant to be capable of and available for work while attending the course. At present, an individual who earnestly takes any kind of job, then applies for and is accepted in a government-sponsored course of instruction which will enable him to better himself and upgrade his capabilities in trade, is bound by the present regulations and must waive his claim for assistance. This is particularly true of students who must attend a provin-cially-sponsored course. Hardship is created because pay is so minuscule that the student cannot even meet minimum living standards. My point is that the commission is therefore hindering the initiative of the individual.
The minister should also consider and explain something else. If it is the aim of his department to help people to upgrade their ability to enter the work force and thus ensure a reduction in the unemployment rate, why has the minister seen fit in the past few years to reduce drastically the number of Manpower seats purchased in vocational and training schools in some parts of Canada? The minister should also take a good look at some of the conditions students must contend with because of the low rates paid to them under provincial rates of pay while they undergo course training.
Another inequity arises under section 25 of the act, which requires the claimant to be capable of, available for and actively seeking work. Let me give you an example of a ridiculous situation in order to demonstrate this hypocrisy. A partially blind citizen of my district was working in a restaurant and had to leave because her husband became sick and required care. When she applied for benefits she was turned down because it was deemed that because of blindness she was not capable of working in a restaurant-even though she had performed her duties for months to the satisfaction of her employer. Similarly, claimants living in isolated areas are disqualified from benefits if they refuse to take a job miles away from where they live. In such cases, after they pay for their travels to and from work, for board, etc., it costs them more to work than it would cost to stay at home or if they did not work. Yet the present system disqualifies them from benefits under the "just cause for refusing to work" provision.
Those examples indicate the weakness in our system, the inflexibility and the lack of individual attention paid by those responsible to Canadians who most need that individual attention. Under the present bill, the government can do whatever it wants with regard to increasing disqualification periods. It can put all it wants into the act on disentitlement. It can put in all the benefit control system it wants. They can keep adding new clauses. They can refer to just causes all they want; but the jusc causes have to be just, and at present it is obvious that they are not.
I was a bit surprised to read in the report of the advisory committee that they were satisfied the benefit control
(Mr. Marshall.]
system was working well. I was even more surprised with the evidence presented by officials of the head office that the benefit control system was working to the benefit of the claimant. This statement of fact indicates a complete lack of recognition of the countless hundreds of thousands of grievances submitted to me and other members of parliament. It proves my point that it is useless to write to the commissioner to inquire into a claim that has been adjudicated against a claimant at the lower level.
It is useless for claimants to appeal their cases. I venture to say that in 99 per cent of the cases-and I am only using a rough figure-the decisions of the local office are turned down. I would like to know the percentage of cases submitted for appeal that were judged in favour of the client, compared with the percentage against.
It is obvious that the purpose of Bill C-69 is to stop the runaway costs of unemployment insurance. It was recently pointed out by a responsible official of an interested group that it is almost impossible to imagine that the cost of our Canadian system is almost equal to that of the United States. When one compares the population figures, something has to be wrong.
It is true, and everyone is aware of this, that as a result of the inefficiency of those responsible for designing the act, rip-offs are occurring. What is really happening is that in the confusion and attempts of the unemployment insurance commission to correct their projections, as pointed out by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), costs have gone beyond the capability of the imagination as to how anyone responsible can be so inadequate that the stopgap measures introduced are hurting the innocent.
To emphasize this point, I refer to the amendment which discriminates against senior citizens and the indignity it inflicts. The government is really saying to those aged 65, "You had better quit working now. You had better stop contributing to Canada. Just stop what you are doing and get out of the mainstream of opportunity, because we do not need you any more. Even though you have been contributing to society and unemployment insurance for many years, we are going to give you $129.28 a month or, if you have a wife and are in need, $419.62 a month." The government thanks them for the contribution and then tells them to get out of the way. For someone receiving a Canada Pension Plan benefit, this is deducted from the amount he is eligible to receive.
I realize that the minister has a tough job to do as a result of the Unemployment Insurance Act that has been developed over the years. He has the important job of having to correct the inequities. I sympathize with him. However, it is surely inexcusable that in his thrust to stop the runaway and rampant cost increases, the low income earner, the underemployed and the aged should be the ones to suffer most. I feel the minister is doing his best and is as concerned as myself and other members about the hurt that will be inflicted on the innocent as a result of the jungle of inequities that exists.
I hope that the referral of the bill at the committee stage, and the subjective and responsible criticisms that have been offered during the second reading debate, will give the minister an opportunity to reflect on those inequities, and that he will consider and introduce further
October 28, 1975

amendments to produce a corrected bill on third reading which will be fair and just to all Canadians.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Andras that Bill C-69, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak in this debate concerning an issue that has been very much to the fore in the last two federal election campaigns. Just a week or two ago someone said it was the politicians who made the Unemployment Insurance Commission an issue in the 1972 campaign. From my experience, I would totally reject that remark. It was made an issue by the people involved. Anyone who was a candidate in the 1972 campaign in the constituency that I represent could not avoid hearing about the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the problems it created. Every time one stopped at a business that was run by a small operator, be it a gas station, restaurant or motel, one had the proprietor of the business crying on his shoulder by the hour about the problems being created for him by the methods and means adopted by the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
As I listened to them throughout that campaign, I realized this was one of the issues that would give the Progressive Conservative Party considerable impetus in the west. As it turned out, it did. Speaking from our own point of view, it was unfortunate that in the subsequent
Unemployment Insurance Act
election of 1974 some of the attention was diverted from that issue to the one that has just been before the House in a rather ironic fashion, namely wage and price controls.
The people about whom I am talking, the class of small entrepreneurs, are seldom given credit by this government for the role they play. Unemployment insurance as it has been constituted in this country has made their role even more difficult. They serve a very useful training function, not as part of any subsidized school system, provincial or federal, but simply as people in small towns, villages and communities who hire local young people to work for them. In the course of that first or second job, these people are trained to function in a gas station, wait at table in a restaurant, or take care of a motel. One of the great frustrations of these entrepreneurs is that following the eight-week training period, the trainee immediately-or soon after-leaves the job, not because he has become terribly efficient at it but to draw unemployment insurance. That is one of the examples I had repeated to me over and over again during that campaign. As one restaurant operator explained to me, it means the loss of fulltime jobs for adults who could be employed full time.
One thing many of these operators have learned is to hire high school students to work part time, because they can keep high school students for two years until they graduate from school to continue their education elsewhere or take jobs with the permanent labour force. They get more out of the training period that way than by hiring employees full-time, only to see them ready to leave after a short while.
One of the reasons I heard a great deal about the more pressing problems connected with unemployment insurance is that my own constituency is one of those gloriously beautiful mountain constituencies embracing some of the finest scenery to be found anywhere in the world. A common complaint made to me concerned the skiing holiday. A person would work half the year, or two-thirds of the year and then, when the snow on the mountains became deep enough to provide good skiing, would leave his or her job and finance his skiing through the Unemployment Insurance Commission, returning to work some time in the spring or when the payments ran out. The skiing holiday paid for by the UIC is something I heard about over and over again. One begins by discounting stories of this kind, thinking them to be invented or exaggerated. But when you hear them over and over again from a variety of ski areas and from people who feel very strongly about these circumstances, you realize they are a key factor in the whole picture.
I shall not comment further on the cost factors involved in this scheme. There has, surely, been an enormous temptation built in to quit a job or to refuse a job which has been offered. It seems to me that a course which ought to be taken and which might return to the Unemployment Insurance Commission a much needed sense of discipline lies in extending the period of time for which a person must work in order to establish eligibility. In recent years we have seen an erosion of the kind of restraint, discipline and loyalty in a work force which used to be an important part of job holding.

October 28, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
I feel that various programs established by the government opposite have contributed to this lack of restraint, this lack of discipline. Too much money has been made available too easily to people in this country. When the decision was made to alter the nature of the unemployment insurance scheme, making it a kind of guaranteed annual income or a scheme for the redistribution of income, both the scheme and the country were in trouble.
There is one group of people in particular to whom I should like to make reference, because even as one criticizes the scheme for being too easy and for permitting people who have worked for only a short period of time to draw benefit for extremely long periods, one must have regard for cases brought to one's attention where real injustice is done to certain people who find themselves disqualified although they know they are entitled to benefit. I am thinking particularly about the older woman, the long-time faithful employee, the one who has never drawn unemployment insurance in her life, the one who has not quit, who has been loyal, who has worked 10, 20 or 25 years, who is laid off through no fault of her own and who finds herself disentitled while knowing from her own experience that others who learned early how to make the system work have been drawing benefits annually or biannually, year after year-they have made a business of getting something out of the scheme.
The older woman I have in mind, brought up in a generation which possessed a somewhat deeper sense of responsibility, a somewhat greater degree of independence, has refused to take advantage of her situation, feeling there would be something wrong about doing so, only to find, in her time of need, when she was laid off and when the reward for being faithful should come to her, that there was really no insurance aspect about the scheme at all. She had merely been paying another tax all those years, a tax that returned nothing except the knowledge that virtue was its own reward in the unemployment insurance business as in other areas of life.
There are certain things I feel the department should not do. It should not promote the break-up of marriages, particularly long-term marriages. It is a common thing in our society for wives to live longer than their husbands and for husbands to retire before their wives are eligible for old age security pensions or retirement pensions. Also, it is a common feature of retirement for families to make a move, often a move from our crowded cities to the countryside or to the smaller towns. Working wives in this position resent the letters they receive telling them they are unemployed voluntarily. And so do I. It seems to me that short of separation or divorce, such a move cannot be avoided by them; it is not the result of any frivolous choice, nor has a job held for a long time been given up as a result of a mere whim. There is too much involved here for the department to put itself in the position of forcing or promoting separation.
Neither should the department involve itself in depopulating small towns. This is something that has been decried in this country for many years. I know it is a natural trend for people today to leave our small centres and go to urban areas, but we do not need any incentive to do so from the Unemployment Insurance Commission. Both sexes do this, but particularly women in small towns

who find themselves unemployed, again through no fault of their own, who apply and are disentitled because they are not prepared to move long distances and resettle in a larger centre. It seems to me they are entitled to some pay-out, having contributed to what is supposed to be an insurance scheme for them.
The Unemployment Insurance Commission should not confuse the search for work with work itself. I find this sort of confusion very prevalent, particularly in the attitude to women who lose their jobs and place their names with Manpower-perhaps there is a certain humour there. These women feel that this should count for something. They search for work with which they are familiar but they are unable to find any, and at that time they become disentitled because they are told that their search has been inadequate.
One case that comes most forcefully to mind concerned someone who was 59 years of age and who had worked in one job for many years. She went to all the equivalent employers in town searching for work, without success. She placed her name with Manpower but was told she had not done enough. She then went through an extended period of time walking up and down the main street of town presenting herself to potential employers. She was in the position of having to tell them that she was 59 years of age but knew nothing about any job they might have. At that point her chances were zero, and the Manpower department knew it. Nevertheless, what they said to her, in effect, was this, "We won't pay you unemployment insurance but we will pay you for the hours that you march up and down the street"-in, of course, a vain search for work. They said, "If you put in enough time, we might consider giving you an entitlement". I feel that kind of treatment is inequitable. It is not the kind of complaint that is made to me by a male worker; it is particularly a feminine problem.
They should not force an applicant into accepting a job below the minimum wage and then disentitle him or her because that job is turned down. I am not a proponent, and never have been, of high minimum wages, and I realize the subject of minimum wages is a sort of sacred cow of our economic system. One does not talk about them much, but if we are going to have them, they must mean something. It seems to me that one of the ultimate indignities to inflict on any woman seeking a job and who turns one down because it pays below the minimum wage is for her then to receive a letter from an official of the UIC telling her that that is the reason she is being disentitled from payments that are hers.
I listened to the speech made last night by the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo) and was disappointed that she did not apply herself to the sort of problem that has been brought to my attention and, I am sure, to the attention of members right across the country. I utterly reject the kind of letter sent by the minister's department stating that an insurance principle is involved here; that when a person contributes to unemployment insurance he is buying a year's insurance, that it is like term insurance with no carry over. I do not follow that reasoning and cannot accept it.
Term or fire insurance have certain specialties about them. For one thing, they are not compulsory, nobody has
October 28, 1975

to buy life insurance or term insurance. You do not have to have fire insurance on your building. You take a chance; if the building burns down you do not collect any insurance. One thing about life insurance, term insurance or any other kind of life insurance is that you collect it only once. But I do not accept that a woman who has paid into a compulsory scheme for 24 years should be told that she cannot collect because there is an insurance principle involved and that she has voluntarily put herself into a position where she cannot find work. She is then at the point when she needs insurance for the very first time, yet when she needs it the most she finds that for her there is no insurance.
In many occupations, sick leave is allowed to accumulate. Then at the end of 35 or 40 years of faithful service, recognition is given that sick leave in the form of a bonus on retirement. I am sure all hon. members know that unemployment insurance is sometimes paid out at the end of a long period as a kind of retirement gift.
I am pleased to see that women are now more militant than they were, but they need to be a lot more militant. I found, when in this House seven years ago, that it was almost impossible to get a woman to take her case to the appeal board. They deemed it an example of throwing good money after bad. Very often a very long trip was involved if a woman did not want to hire a lawyer to present her case for her, or could not afford to do so. She would hear from others that it was a hopeless cause anyway, that she would not get anything even if she did appeal, and as a result it was very difficult to persuade a woman to take her case to the first board of appeal.
I am very happy to see that women are now more prepared to appeal their case, but even so there are problems. In addition, I am concerned about the number of women who sit on appeal boards across the country; the women still tend to get turned down pretty regularly. During the summer recess I was talking to one woman who had written to me and told me she had been reinstated. She said there were at least six others in the same position but they would not appeal their case, so I suspect that those who do appeal are just the tip of the iceberg. The problem is that once the appeal has gone against them, they cannot take the matter to the umpire because the only person who can pass the appeal on is the chairman of the very board that turned the appeal down. I find such people are very reluctant to send to the umpire a case on which they have given a negative ruling. It seems to me there could be some reform undertaken there which would make the umpire more truly an umpire than that official is at the present time.
There is another area on which I should like to spend a little time. It is a little different than what I have been discussing. I listened with interest last evening as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Portelance) spoke. He talked about the decision to take anyone over age 65 out of the scheme altogether. The excuse he gave is most interesting. As recorded at page 8593 of Hansard he mentioned there are other programs for elderly people, and then said:
Unemployment Insurance Act
Considering all those improvements, the programs would unnecessarily overlap if persons having age 65 were still covered by the unemployment insurance plan.
That is a laugh. At one time Manpower and the UIC were one. The decision was made in the 27th Parliament to divorce the two. If there are any bureaux or offices which overlap they are the Manpower offices and the Unemployment Insurance Commission. If the Unemployment Insurance Commission is so concerned about overlapping then I suggest action be taken, as quickly as possible, to put the two parts of what should be one body back together again. That would end the overlap that is there.
It might also end the other factor where a person who puts his or her name in at the Manpower office, assuming that has some meaning, finds that not even the Unemployment Insurance Commission pays any attention to that. The woman who puts her name in at the Manpower office is told that her search for work is inadequate. This is one of the scandals in the way the Manpower offices and Unemployment Insurance Commission offices operate at the present time. So, I find it all a little amusing when the parliamentary secretary refers to an overlapping. The only thing which counts these days at a time of double digit inflation in Canada when one is over 65 is dollars and cents.
I would like to know, and I would like to know if the department knows, whether the senior citizens of 65 years of age will be better off by this change. That is the only argument to justify it. We need some figures to tell us whether that is true.
I can well believe the second part of the parliamentary secretary's speech when he said it is almost impossible to apply effectively the provisions of the law pertaining to availability and active search for a job to persons of that age since a great many of them are no longer members of the labour force. That goes along with the argument I presented earlier. I contend that that sentence has been applied by the Unemployment Insurance Commission for a very long time to the woman between age 55 and age 65. She is the one who has found it almost impossible to convince the commission that she is part of the labour force any longer. God knows, if the fact that she is in that age category is a problem, then the problem for those over age 65 must be almost insurmountable. One thing which may make it easier for them might be an extension in the period required for eligibility because that extension would show their connection to the labour force more clearly than anything else.
There is another thing about which I wonder. What would happen to the employer who employs only people over age 65? Would he or she be freed of the obligation of paying anything into the unemployment insurance scheme, and how long could that employer function? I am sure there are many employers who could get along very nicely for long periods with a staff composed entirely of people over age 65. The savings to them in not having to contribute anything to the scheme would be significant. I should like to know whether any thought has been given to that. These days one knows that the margin between profit and loss for a great many businesses, especially small businesses, is not the market but rather the government and its various forms of taxation required of companies.

October 28, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
I think I would have more respect for the parliamentary secretary if he had said in his remarks that this action had to be taken to make those people over age 65 more employable by offering that sort of negative bonus to anyone who employed them, since they would no longer have to continue any share to the UIC. If that was the reason behind it, it would make some sense. However, if it is the other way arround and the real reason is to divorce them further from any hope of being hired, and in effect they are being told they should not clutter up the employment picture and should not cause headaches to the UIC in determining whether or not they are truly part of the work force, that would really be a negative aspect of this part of the bill because, it seems to me, that if we can encourage our senior citizens to function normally and usefully in our society we should do so.
I should like to have a clear explanation of the reasons. I should like to hear the minister, or someone from his department, tell me that this change will mean more money in the hands of people over age 65, because if it means there will be less for them, this is not the time to introduce that step since inflation has eroded the position of these people to a very great extent, and there are too many of them who for too long have paid the price of inflation.
So, Madam Speaker, while there are some parts of this bill which meet with approval it is not the total second look at the Unemployment Insurance Commission that this party promised during the last election campaign. That was one of the issues on which we campaigned. Were we elected there would be a total review by a royal commission, I believe, of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. That is what I believe is needed at the present time, a very serious and a very top level lengthy re-thinking of the whole matter so that representations could be heard from anyone with an interest in it, and so that there could be representations from women's groups, senior citizens, and the working men of this country.
I have a feeling that what we are doing now is tinkering with the scheme, and that the effect of the passage of this bill will be not to improve the scheme but rather to work hardships on some of the people who can least afford to have any more hardship thrust upon them.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was very interested in the speech made by the minister as well as in the speech of the hon. member who is the candidate for the Ontario Liberal leadership, and I was particularly interested in the simple facts which both stressed and the others which they overlooked. They stressed the abuses of the Unemployment Insurance Act and the fact that the government has had to make payments in excess of what was necessary, and so they wanted to strengthen the benefit control section.
Yet the minister, in talking about this bill, never referred to the fact that 4 per cent unemployment is totally unacceptable to the majority of thinking Canadians, and that probably even 2 per cent unemployment would be a higher unemployment rate in Canada than most people would want to accept. What the minister said in effect was that because the government has not been

able to provide employment for Canadians, it wants to divest itself of this responsibility and lay it on the shoulders of the working people and of the employers, with the result that unemployment will probably be raised to 6 per cent. This year it will be around 5 per cent, but with the record of this government it is foreseeable that it will be 6 per cent or 7 per cent, and that it will continue to grow.
That is really what we should be talking about, namely, what we should do to solve the problems of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. The easiest way to solve these problems is to provide employment for all Canadians. The people in my area are no different from the people in the minister's area. His people also are unemployed seasonally and are not able to find full employment. They look to unemployment insurance as a stopgap because the government has not been fair to them in providing a climate of full employment. When there are jobs, they work; when there are no jobs they would like to get some assistance, but they do not want that assistance to be paid entirely to them; they want all the people of the country to share in the responsibility.
We considered that it was a complete distortion of the principle to have the floor based on 4 per cent unemployment, and now the minister has based it on a sliding scale so that there is no incentive to stop unemployment from growing, and no incentive for the government to provide full employment.
We hear members saying that there are abuses of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Sure there are abuses. There are abuses among my constituents in Timiskaming, although not many. There have been some frauds that have been reported, and action has been taken on them. I am sure the same is true in the riding of my colleague, the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), and even in the minister's own riding in northern Ontario, but what prospects do we have as Canadians?
A question was asked this afternoon in the House about the six Canadians who reportedly stole $4 million and are now enjoying themselves in the sunshine. Is the government worried about that? Has it sent anyone down to try to do anything about that? No, but it would surely send someone 200 or 300 miles to Timiskaming, Thunder Bay, or Geraldton, or any of these places in the hinterland, to look for some little guy who may have taken three days off to go hunting when he was supposed to be looking for work. When it is all settled, they will take away from him unemployment insurance for the three days, and then they will find out he was looking for work on the other days.
No one considers the cost of having a benefit control officer travel 200 or 300 miles and of his being wined and dined. He may be away two or three days and then he may have a great report written up when he comes back, because many places to which he went are hardly on the map and he has never been there before, but he has been wined and dined at the expense of the taxpayers. I have had difficulty myself in getting to some of these places on occasion.
There are many roads around there and many communities in the bush area where roads go in all directions. You can drive for five or six miles and finally see the same shack or the same building, and then you know you are going around in circles. There are no real roads in these

areas, but the benefit control officer will try to go there to catch a person and then find he is not able to look after himself. But everybody is quite proud of him. The minister has mentioned that there have been 250,000 disqualifications out of ten million claims. Is that very many?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: It is two million.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Let us say it is two million, although I doubt whether the minister is right. In my opinion there are not that many disqualifications because it is a simple fact about unemployment insurance that those who continue to abuse the system know the rules and do not get into any trouble.
The previous hon. member who spoke referred to a lady who went down the street to every place on the street asking for a job although she knew she was not employable in that community and she knew every job available there. After she had gone 10 or 12 times to the same employers asking them for a job, which they had already told her they did not have, she knew there was nothing more to do and that she could not get a job even if these employers needed someone. That is a fact.
Our bureaucracy is stupid because the officials know all about this, and the commission has been told about this many times. They know they could telephone Manpower and find out if there are any jobs in Geraldton for a woman who had been employed for a considerable period of time in the office of the local lumber company and was then laid off. They would know there are no jobs for women in that category in Geraldton. They do not need to have her traipse around to a hotel looking for the job of a waitress because those jobs are also filled. Yet they still disqualify her if she has not gone to five or six places in that week looking for a job, although she knows there is no job for her there, and the stupid officials know that also.
Everyone involved knows that, and yet they continue to say she has to go to these six places again. Quite often they are so dumb that they will telephone to ask if she has been to a certain place. We should not treat people who are looking for work as if they had no brains at all, and yet that is what these officials do. We really do not do much for them as a government either when we say to people they have to look for a job in a certain area even though Manpower says there is no work there.
The previous speaker mentioned-and perhaps the minister was not listening so I will repeat it-that one of the things that the minister must do if he is going to do anything to improve the unemployment situation, to improve the functioning of the Unemployment Insurance Commission, and to improve the functioning of Manpower, is to put those two agencies together. The present minister without portfolio (Mr. Marchand) is the cause of the division of these departments. At one time he had one of the departments under him and he did not want the other one, so they broke them up and created a new department. That department should never have been broken up.
I remember going to the offices in the old set-up. One went to one side-perhaps the minister knows this, but if he does not I will repeat it-if you were looking for a job, and if you could not find it you went over to the other side where they accepted your application for benefits and where they paid you your benefits. The next week you
Unemployment Insurance Act
would be back looking for a job there, and if there were no jobs the same people who were handling both divisions would speak to each other and know what your situation was, so one hand knew what the other was doing. When the departments were divided, orders were given that the officials should not talk to each other. Manpower was not to help fill out an unemployment insurance form. Unemployment Insurance was to have nothing to do with employment.
What has happened? The minister knows what the problem is because he has played around with the hiring set up, and he has in fact placed a number of people. I believe he said the other day that his department, through unemployment insurance, had placed 45,000 people in jobs. I give him full credit for doing that, but the minister will have failed the Canadian people, those looking for jobs and those who apply for benefits, if he does not unite those two functions and connect the person who is looking for benefits with the agency which can supply him with a job or inform him that there are no jobs available. If there are no jobs available, he should receive benefits. If there are jobs, then he should take a job.
We are not interested in defending people who abuse the system, but we are less interested in defending a system which is stupid, and the system is often plain stupid. One of the reasons why I say that is that we, as members of parliament, know particular areas, the peculiarities of particular communities, the employment picture in those communities, and the transportation facilities. When we bring that information to the insurance appeal officer after a case has gone through the appeal structure and all of the crap that it must go through, and he has that new information, he makes the right decision and the person is reinstated.
This raises the whole problem of appeals. A person appealing without the help of a union, some other official, a lawyer, or a member of parliament, cannot go to a tribunal with any hope of winning his case. If he could, all he would need to do is write out the reason why he thinks he should not be disqualified. That is sent to the insurance officer who considers it, and if that information is sufficient to override the information which warranted the disqualification, he will cancel it.
I can honestly say that in my years of dealing with unemployment insurance, and particularly in the last seven or eight years, I have developed a great respect for the insurance officers of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. I have seldom seen information given to an insurance officer when it came through on appeal, or when it became public information at a hearing, which would have justified a decision other than the decision made by the insurance officer.
I wrote a letter to a judge some time ago, to which I did not receive a reply. He was on a tribunal, and I told him what I thought of him and the system because he simply sat on that tribunal and endorsed the decision which had been made, without any means of deciding whether the claimant had any justification for appealing his disqualification. The claimant had no ability to appeal. He just said that he was entitled and therefore appealed, and the judge

Unemployment Insurance Act
took that and made his decision on it. He is dishonest and could not possibly be a judge. How can one judge after hearing only one side of a case?
We have discussed this with the chairman of the commission, and he is quite interested in setting ip an appellate agency. I am not in favour of setting it up on a legal basis where there are lawyers involved, but I believe that if we have the money to send out a benefit control officer to disadvantage a claimant further when the claimant feels he has already been treated unjustly and unfairly, the tribunal should at least have the right to send out an official to ask the claimant on what basis he believes he was unjustly treated so that on that basis it can be decided whether the claimant is entitled to transportation, whether he has been looking for work, or whether there should be someone to care of the claimant's baby if it is a maternity benefit. Surely it is not asking too much for that judge, who says he is an honourable person, to hear the claimant's side of the story.
The minister is doing a great job. He has provided for transportation, but transportation is not really important. Why should claimants go through the process of sitting in Sudbury all day, driving 250 miles, perhaps staying in a hotel room, and listening to many cases which he cannot understand? The procedure was very formal when I was there, and very like a courtroom. They might as well wear gowns and wigs. Obviously there are people there asking nasty questions with a view to calling claimants liars because they have already been disqualified. The claimant has already met the benefit control officer, and that is enough of an experience for most people.
We have been through this before. Everyone knows that this tribunal is a farce. Going to an umpire should not be allowed unless it is on a case of law. I do not think there should be an appeal unless there is an allegation of dishonesty. I am not prepared to say that there is dishonesty. I think these people are incompetent, but I do not think they are dishonest.
I will say to the whole country that I think the labour representatives on most of the tribunals are a damned disgrace; that they do not represent the claimant any better than the employer, and in some cases are worse than the company. They become part of that little club. They meet every few days, and have nice little meetings. I know some of these people personally. I worked with some of them, I was in the same union with some of them, and I have told them that I think it is a disgrace. They do not ask questions which should be asked, on behalf of the claimant, even when the claimant is there. Madam Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the supper hour I was raising with the minister the problems we are having in relation to appeals and the appeal tribunal. I tried to make the point that I have tried to make in the last number of years since unemployment insurance was separated from the national employment agency. I think most people will agree that there was a good deal of merit in the procedure when one went and reported to the employment agency and asked for a job. If no job was available you just went over to the other side and collected your benefits. There was a very clear relationship between the job market and the availability of benefits.
The system we have now hardly takes the employment agency into consideration, and while it is true that in order to draw unemployment insurance benefits you must be registered with Manpower there does not seem to be any relationship between the functions of paying benefits and providing employment.
We have had seven or eight years to see the mistakes that arose from separating our employment policy and our unemployment insurance benefits. It seems to me that the minister has an obligation to consider what the public believes to be an abuse when the person drawing benefits is not really looking for work. The system reflects detrimentally on the rural areas, particularly those where no employment is available. It is foolish to disqualify people on the basis that they are not actively seeking work when they know full well that there is no work.
Two clauses in the present bill will have to be given a new interpretation. One of them is "just cause"-I think the minister referred to it as "good reason". Just cause has not been interpreted as a simple, good reason. The application has been very strict and very detrimental, and many people seeking unemployment insurance benefits are being hurt.
The second problem arises with the average person who says that the people drawing benefits are not looking for work. An argument used by many small employers is that they cannot afford to hire anybody because the unemployment insurance benefits are too high. I think the minister has an obligation to see that the minimum wage paid for menial jobs and unorganized occupations is at least as high as unemployment insurance benefits. In many cases there is the legitimate complaint that people will not work in a certain plant because they can draw more from unemployment insurance benefits than they would earn. I do not think unemployment insurance should pay more than the minimum wage, and in a modern society the obvious solution to that problem is to increase the minimum wage to compare favourably with unemployment insurance benefits.
There was a former member of this House who never impressed me very much until I heard him explain unemployment insurance one night, and that was the late Joe Habel. He said that if you paid insurance on your car for 20 or 30 years as he had, and never collected on it, that was a good thing because it meant you never had an accident. Using that principle, if you pay unemployment insurance and do not collect, that means you have never been unemployed. From my point of view that is an ideal condition.
To reduce the age to 65 is commendable, but it raises a number of problems. I have talked to a number of people
October 28, 1975

who work for the railroad and in other places and who face mandatory retirement at 65 even though their physical or mental condition does not really require it. They can work and want to work. They know nothing else.
I suggest that the minister and the department will need to consider the question of retirement itself. In this country there are no federal or provincial programs to qualify people for retirement. In future people will not retire at age 65. Retirement age will be reduced to age 60, and even lower, as automation and computers play an ever larger role in our lives. No longer will people work from the age of 14 or 15 until 70 or 75. They will enter the labour force in their 20's and retire at 60. Unless they retire early other people who want to enter the labour market will not find jobs. Therefore we must create programs which will train people for retirement.
Interestingly, railroaders retire at age 65, but, on average, live no more than two years after retirement. One day they are operating the train on the run they have known all their working lives, and the next day they are retired with nothing to do. I think it is wrong to cut off unemployment insurance benefits at age 65. Under this legislation, it will become mandatory for people to retire at age 65.
It is no good telling any man to retire if you have not introduced some kind of program which will train him for his retirement and allow him to pursue some interest, some hobby or recreational activity which will occupy his time. I suppose railroaders are a particular group, as they sleep and eat at odd hours, knowing they can be called at any time of day or night. They have so many hours to reply to the call, or book off sick; otherwise they must work. Their lifestyle does not allow for social activities of the sort enjoyed by people with normal working hours. Consequently retirement weighs more heavily on them than it does on others. One can see that we are creating great difficulties if we insist on retiring people at age 65.
