speechtext: Right on.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I believe we are obligated to train people for retirement, to allow them to pursue meaningful activities. Yet really this bill says that after age 65 you are no longer on the labour market. Clearly we must help people who must retire because of age but whose physical and mental condition enables them to go on working. The bill says that they are not entitled to unemployment insurance after age 65. We must remember that not all people who reach 65 or 70 want to retire. Some find it difficult to retire. For that reason the government must act. So far it has lacked the courage or desire to institute training programs which will help people in their retirement.
May I now say a word about manpower programs. I remember a program known as program 5 under which people could train for various occupations, and the standards were applied nationally. Training was provided with a view to employment, beginning often at high school level. The program continued in that manner until Quebec kicked up a fuss about control, as it was entitled to do under the constitution.
As I say, the standards applying to subjects taught under program 5 applied right across the country. That
Unemployment Insurance Act
meant that if you trained as a plumber in Ontario, you could work as as a plumber in British Columbia, Nova Scotia, or pretty well anywhere else in the country, because the federal government was instrumental in providing the jobs, and that federal program trained people to meet job requirements. We were well on the way to establishing national standards. I raise this point for this reason that our manpower centres do not always send employers qualified employees. Take the case of the truck driver.
I remember an experiment which was tried by the Manpower office in my area, in conjunction with Simard Beaudry, who was working on a large project. The office put pressure on him to accept truck drivers they sent to him. Simard Beaudry put those men in a large truck and said, "If you can drive the truck, you can have the job; if you cannot drive the truck, you are not a truck driver". It turned out that most applicants could not drive heavy construction trucks. They had driven half ton trucks on the farm, but they are completely different from the sort of trucks used during the construction of a large dam.
Usually the Department of Manpower office cannot assure the employer that the applicant sent to the job is qualified. As a result, Manpower offices have fallen into disrepute with employers. Under program 5, the employment office could assure the employer of the employee's qualifications, because the department was in the position to train the employee, and did. That is no longer the case.
We must make many changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act. Certainly abuses should be eliminated, but it is unfair to expect people living in high unemployment areas to go without benefits for six weeks, on grounds that they may be ripping off the system. Clearly we must change the act, to provide benefits immediately to those who are truly seeking work but cannot find it. I think the minister is well aware of this problem. I am surprised that so far he has done nothing about it.
Another problem concerns the definition of suitable employment. What is suitable employment? For instance, what is suitable employment for a teacher who cannot renew a contract? Is her suitable employment work as a clerk in a store? After four or five weeks, does she have to take that kind of job at the minimum wage because she is not able to get a contract as a teacher at a fairly good salary?
I think this "suitable employment" has been badly abused. Surely we can work out some kind of system that allows a person to drop his standard as the months go by. It may be in this country that unemployment will go so high that people will be glad to dig ditches because there is no other job available to them, no matter what their education or ability may be.
I remember the last depression. We hired someone to work on the farm who had an electrical engineering degree from Queen's University. That young fellow worked on the farm for $25 a month plus room and board, and he was glad to get the job. He left shortly after that. My father was instrumental in getting him a job with Northern-Hydro in Quebec. He started as an oiler and within a few months he was running one of their plants. The next time I saw him he was in charge of the Common-

October 28, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
wealth program at the electrical school at St. Thomas. He was responsible for the electrical training of airforce personnel. It was not because he did not have the ability or education that he was glad to work for $25 a month on the farm.
If the Liberal government stays in power long enough it may be that suitable employment will be building an airport for ten cents a day, plus tobacco once a week, and a pair of pants when you can scrounge them. That is what some people received during the last depression. That is not what we are hoping will happen, but is the kind of criteria being used now for those who are unemployed. Those who are unemployed today are having just as difficult a time in making an adjustment as people did during the depression. When you ask someone to go from a good paying job, without the opportunity of having a reasonable period to obtain similar employment, to a job that does not pay nearly as well, you really are not doing anything for them.
Many people are in favour of any change that will cut down the number of people on unemployment insurance. If it were up to those who are complaining about minor abuses by those seeking unemployment insurance, I am sure they would be very much in favour of supporting the proposition of having full employment in this country.
This change in the act will remove the ceiling, floor, or whatever it is called, the 4 per cent benchmark of unemployment insurance. It says in effect that the government and the private sector will participate in the extended benefits, but up to the 4 per cent level it will be the responsibility of the employer and the employee. I remember when that 4 per cent was put in there. It was considered at that time that a reasonable level of unemployment would be 2 per cent. It has now been raised to considerably above 4 per cent. It is on a sliding scale. The minister said that, as far as his government is concerned, unemployment not only is going to be with us but will increase, and the workers with their employers will have to carry the.,unemployment insurance fund.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I welcome this opportunity to participate in this debate on the Unemployment Insurance Commission. We have a good unemployment insurance plan in this country and we must continually strive to make it better.
Unemployment insurance is important. All Canadians recognize that. Some say it is being abused. Obviously that is so in some cases, but I think it is in the minority of cases. It is to be hoped that the amendments now before us will rectify some of those abuses. However, in my riding, Mr. Speaker, unemployment insurance is used rather than abused, and used to a great degree because we have one of the highest rates of unemployment in Canada, with well over 20 per cent. Many of my people depend on unemployment insurance and will continue to do so for some time to come. They depend on it because in most cases their occupations are seasonal, and for a portion of the year there is no cash income. That is not to say that they are idle.
The people of my riding are not afraid of work and never have been. There is adequate evidence to show that Newfoundlanders and Labradorians have always been a proud and independent people, a self-reliant people who have worked hard for a living. They still want to work

hard for a living. I do not believe for a minute that they want to exist solely on handouts. They want to work, and in fact surveys show that the work ethic is strong all across the country. In spite of the fact that we have a relatively high rate of unemployment, I feel that most of those people are not working through no fault of their own. I believe the majority want jobs and will take jobs when we offer them.
Unemployment insurance is the first line of defence against unemployment, but the best form of defence is often attack. I think this was referred to by some speakers before the supper break and, indeed, afterwards. That is the case here. Unemployment insurance can only be clearly seen in relation to its more important counterpart, employment insurance. This is the most important phrase. That is the key phrase that sums up the philosophy that we should be pursuing and that we are pursuing, for one of the great successes of this government and the Department of Manpower and Immigration, of which the Unemployment Insurance Commission is a partner, is its job creation programs.
The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) referred to the split-off in the department of the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the difficulty of integrating the two aspects of the department. I want to tell him that those two branches are working very closely together. In fact Manpower and the Unemployment Insurance Commission in many cases work as one.
The evidence of this is the Newfoundland project where over a two-year period about 2,000 unemployed, including people chronically on unemployment insurance and people on welfare, are being given positive training in vocational schools and in industry while they continue to receive unemployment insurance. This project recognizes that a defence against unemployment is not enough, and that there must be attack. It recognizes that it is not enough to keep people, because in many cases this means keeping them down, keeping them in a rut, keeping them in a section of society which has the welfare syndrome. Those chronically unemployed are often there not because they do not want to work, or because they are lazy. There are some in that category, it is true, but I do not believe they are in the majority. I believe a great many of the unemployed are thus because they are disabled for some reason, or because they do not have the skills or the education to get and hold meaningful jobs.
Many people, more and more in fact, are getting caught in the rapidly changing job patterns caused by advancing technology. The machine age is rolling right along, but in its path it is crushing many men and women who formerly trained for years to gain a marketable skill. Therefore we must continually improve and expand our training programs because in the long run I believe that it is only through these training and retraining programs, together with our job creation programs, that we can deal effectively with the unemployment problem.
The Newfoundland project is an attempt at this type of training and retraining. It is a unique experiment wherein those receiving unemployment insurance are placed in training programs according to their skill level and their expectations. Manpower tops off unemployment insurance where necessary and provides other programs of its own, such as travel and housing allowances. This project is
October 28, 1975

being monitored closely, and hopefully it can be implemented elsewhere in Canada. It illustrates that the UIC is not simply a body which hands out cheques. This project shows that they are interested in the growth and development of people. I can attest to that, having worked closely with the commission. A great deal of credit is due the commission for the positive attitude it has fostered in its administrators and its employees, and credit is due to its chairman for the dedicated way in which he has worked toward this end.
There are other success stories in job creation-the attack on unemployment at its source. The LIP program is a Godsend to a province like Newfoundland and Labrador, and to a riding like mine where work is largely seasonal. If members of the House could come to my riding and see the projects which have been completed by men and women who would otherwise be unemployed they would appreciate the value of the program. I can show them community halls, slipways, wharves, breakwaters, town halls, roads and many other things-things they regard as essential- which otherwise they would not have. The only difficulty is that there is never enough money to fund the many worthwhile projects in communities which desperately need them.
Even though my riding received $1.5 million this year there were still projects turned down in communities where there will be no other work this winter, and where men and women will have to get by on unemployment insurance or welfare. The fact is, of course, that the federal government will be funding many of these people in one way or another. I believe that what we should do is to design a winter works program along the lines of the
project now going on in Newfoundland so that people are not simply kept but are doing something meaningful in return for the money they receive. I believe they want this. There are always many times the number of applications we can fund under LIP. People want to work; they want to improve their community. We are spending federal money in these communities anyway, so their potential should be put to a positive end.
An even more successful program within the department is LEAP. I believe that in the long run this program has more potential than LIP when it comes to alleviating chronic unemployment. I should like to refer to many projects which are now under way but I will confine myself to mentioning three which are now in progress in my riding where this program is well on its way to solving the chronic unemployment problem.
It is a program which gives people training on the job, plus a chance to become productive in the long run and acquire skills which will be marketable for years to come. I am thinking, for example, of 13 farmers in the Green Bay area who have been working under a LEAP program; their wages have been paid for two years and at the end of the coming year they can go on to become self-supporting. I am thinking, too, about a boat building project, and about a fishing operation under the LEAP program. Each of them represents a meaningful attack on the problem of unemployment.
Unemployment Insurance Act
A further program which is at work in my riding is the community employment strategy. This is presently operating in the southern portion of Labrador in my province, where a number of communities have organized under the guidance of the job creation branch of the Department of Manpower and Immigration to determine the directions in which government programs of all kinds are succeeding or failing, where amendments or modifications should be made to them, and where new programs are needed. These people are attempting to decide for themselves what resources they possess, what kind of jobs can reasonably be created in their communities, what help is needed, and what training or skill development is needed.
The main point here is that government, hopefully, will become what it ought to be-the servant of the people. The people will decide where they are going and how they will get there. And government will give them support, and follow in the direction they wish to take. This is decentralization of decision-making taken to its extreme. But it is absolutely the right approach. For once the local people have an opportunity to make the bureaucracy work for them. It is still too early to assess the situation, but the initial signs are good and I am hoping the strategy will work. It must work if we are to attack chronic unemployment effectively.
I have tried to show that there must be not simply a defence against unemployment but an attack upon unemployment. Unemployment insurance and other funds coming from the government can be used in a meaningful way, not simply to keep people going but to get them back as productive citizens. So the best defence, to my mind, is attack. This does not mean, however, that we do not need defence. Unemployment insurance is the first line of defence against unemployment, the first defence against temporary loss of income. Hon. members might note that word temporary. It is not a defence against permanent loss of income. We have other means of looking after the elderly, the disabled, and single parent families. This is an insurance plan against temporary unemployment and in that sense it is like any other term insurance plan.
I note too that the hon. member for Timiskaming referred to this aspect in his speech and remarked that if, at the end of his career, a worker had paid into the scheme without deriving any monetary return from it he could get some satisfaction at least from the fact that he had never lost his job. Unemployment insurance is an insurance plan, and it is like term insurance plans. Now the premium to be charged is going up, as are the premiums of other insurance plans. But I do not see how we can avoid this if the tripartite nature of the plan is to be retained.
From the beginning the unemployment insurance plan has been tripartite in concept. When it was developed in 1940 the administration of the act was entrusted to a commission composed of a chief commissioner, a commissioner representing employers, and one representing employees. This arrangement, symbolizing the tripartite nature of the plan, has persisted to the present day. There are three partners-the employees, the employers, and the government.
A partnership arrangement was set up which provided that the employer and the employee would pay an equal

October 28, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
contribution, and that the government would pay an additional amount equal to 20 per cent of the sum collected from employers and employees. In addition the government was to pay for the administration of the program. In 1962 the Gill Committee recommended that the costs of benefits be shared equally by employers and employees, and that there be no contribution by the general taxpayer toward the basic insurance plan. This idea is carried to an extreme in the United States where employers pay the entire cost of the insurance plan, with the exception of extended benefits during periods of very high unemployment. These benefits are totally paid by the state or federal governments.
In this country, however, the original principle of tripartite participation has been retained. It has been altered, though, so that the government might adjust its share of the cost to varying rates of national employment. What is really being proposed in the present instance is a similar operation. But in this case, as in previous cases, the government will pay for benefits extended due to high regional or national rates of unemployment.
What is being proposed is a change in the threshold of 4 per cent. The proposal is that the threshold not be fixed but that it be made flexible and allowed to rise and fall with the national unemployment rate. This principle of coupling thresholds and limits to moving averages which reflect current trends is one that is followed elsewhere, for example, in the calculation of the old age pension, in salary matters, in cost of living clauses, in family allowances. What is proposed now is to apply this principle to premiums paid for unemployment insurance.
It should be noted that the calculation of maximum insurable earnings, and therefore the maximum benefit payable, is based now on an eight year moving average of the industrial composite wage index. Here again the principle of limits being tied to a moving average reflecting economic trends is evident. It would seem reasonable, therefore, that the calculation of the participation of the private sector in the program should be made in a similar way.
The tripartite arrangement for sharing the cost of the unemployment insurance program is an extremely good one. It provides for the active participation by both employers and employees in a program which benefits them both, while at the same time providing for the federal government to acknowledge its effect on the labour market through its monetary and fiscal policy, and thus on the cost of unemployment insurance benefits.
The proposal in Bill C-69 to relate the threshold at which government participation starts more realistically to prevailing economic conditions is consistent with this tripartite formula. It reflects the principles embodied in the 1971 legislation which state that the private sector should be expected to pay the basic costs of the scheme which are more directly related to insurance, and the government should assume responsibility for those costs which are more in the nature of income transfer or income support.
The proposed eight year moving average threshold rate will not only reinforce these principles but will also provide for an automatic adjustment in the participation

formula which can respond to changing economic conditions. The only alternative, of course, would have been an increase in taxes, drawing the additional cost of the program from general tax revenues, which again would be a departure from the user-pay principle and would impose upon people who did not use the plan the cost of the plan. Besides that, I believe that the major increase in cost will be borne by the employers, not in fact by the employees, certainly not those in the lower income brackets.
There are other amendments to the act that I think are good in principle, and on which I should like to comment. One increases the penalty for those who quit their jobs for no good reason. This idea is good in principle. The waiting time is being doubled. Although it is a good idea in principle, I hope that the application of it in some areas will be with an understanding of local conditions.
For example, there are many people in my riding who have no choice but to work away from home since there are no local jobs for them. In many of these cases they leave their families at home while they go away for many months at a time to areas far away. I would not want to do that and I do not think many members of this House would either. I can understand why men would want to leave a job under those conditions, especially if housing is inadequate and the amenities of life that they expect to find in the communities are not there. So I think, generally speaking, the penalty for quitting a job without good reason is a sound principle; but let us get at the cause rather than at the symptom.
I think we can solve a lot of these problems if in northern and remote communities, and in industrially rich communities, we do provide proper housing and amenities. If that is the case and these men can take their families with them they would have no reason to quit the job. We must examine the cause of why a person quits his job, and come up with a solution, such as the provision of proper housing.
I am also glad to see the amendment that would provide unemployment insurance benefits to sponsors of LIP and LEAP projects. Quite often in small rural communities the sponsors of such projects are in fact themselves unemployed. I have had cases in the past in my own riding where sponsors of LIP projects did not receive unemployment insurance benefits, so there is very little incentive for them to apply for them in the first place.
Another matter I want to mention is that raised by my colleague, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall), namely, unemployment insurance for fishermen. At the present time fishermen feel discriminated against. They cannot draw unemployment insurance benefits for as long as other workers; the maximum is something like 23 weeks, with eight weeks of contribution. Other workers can draw almost 51 weeks.
I know the history of this plan and why it is this way. I think there are inequities in it, and I agree with my colleague who spoke this afternoon that the fishermen are not fairly treated. They cannot draw benefits until December. A fisherman may finish work in September, for example, but he cannot draw unemployment insurance benefits until December. Thereafter he can draw them until May, but not after May, yet the fishing season may not open until June or July. These inequities in the program must be remedied.
October 28, 1975

We have been working to change them, but not within the unemployment insurance program. The Minister of State (Fisheries) (Mr. LeBlanc) has promised to bring into the House this winter, during this session, an income support plan for the fisheries. It would be meaningless to make amendments at the present time to the bill on behalf of the fishermen, much as they are needed, when this plan is in the offing. The best we can do is to wait for the fishermen's income support plan to be brought in by the Minister of State (Fisheries), and hopefully we can get it through parliament and in effect before the next fishing season. The present unemployment insurance scheme for fishermen is with us now for this year, bad as it is, but having lived with it for this long we can live with it for a few more months until the new income support plan is put in place.
I do not want to go into the details of this new plan and what it contains; that will come in a later debate. I recognize the problem is a real and serious one. The fishermen have been waiting patiently for the new plan and they must be given meaningful help. We must have a new scheme or we can say goodbye to the inshore fishery. The fishermen must be adequately supported during the off season, and they are not at the present time.
These are difficult times. Like all countries in the world, we are experiencing economic difficulty. One of the effects of that difficulty is an unemployment rate that is unacceptable. It is doubly important, therefore, that we ensure that we have an unemployment insurance plan that guards against erosion of the work ethic while at the same time it provides adequate protection to people when and as they need it. I welcome the flexibility that these amendments introduce into the plan. I believe they will be for the better and will improve the service that the plan provides to our people.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I begin my contribution to this debate on the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act of 1971, I must say I took some interest in the remarks of my hon. friend from Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador. He heaped high accolades upon these amendments, the unemployment insurance program as it now exists, and the job creation program of the government which as he says operates in conjunction with this unemployment insurance program. If I remember correctly, his statement was that unemployment insurance is the first line of defence against unemployment.
However, prior to this the government had created a lot of work programs to help the worker in his every day life. It rather reminds me of the boy scout who was very late home from school. As the evening grew longer and it got dark his mother became very worried that he was not home. Finally after dinner he showed up. His mother asked him why he was home from school so late, and he said that he had been helping this little old lady across the street. So his mother said: "Well, what took so long?" He replied: "Well, she didn't want to go".
That is the impression I get of the government and its program. It parades around like a boy scout helping out everyone, but helping them out in ways in which they do not want to be helped. It seems to me that part of the problem with our economy is that the government is so
Unemployment Insurance Act
busy trying to help people out that it will not let them help themselves. If the government would let them help themselves, the economy would be far ahead of where it is today.
I am pleased that the minister is bringing forward these amendments. I have a great deal of regard for him and I think he is trying to do a good piece of work in his portfolio. He has been given a sizeable job by his predecessor and he has a lot of cleaning up to do. So I not only admire him, I feel sorry for him in the work that he has to do.
In a sense I have no quarrel with the need for some of these amendments. In some cases I suspect they do not go far enough. But it is encouraging to find the government realizing that there is a need to upgrade the UIC program. I would seriously question the timing of the legislation, coming as it does in a period when we have 7.2 per cent of the work force unemployed. It seems that the minister is changing the rules of the game right in the middle of the game. The government engaged in a program of overindulgence and over-generous policy for a number of years while we had high employment, during which time it encouraged workers to assume that benefits would come continuously. Any time a worker became unemployed there would only be a short waiting period, if any waiting period at all, before he would be in the chips again. Many people never prepared themselves for a period of extended unemployment such as they are facing today. Yet the government adopted an attitude of paternalism toward the worker, an attitude of encouraging dependency on government. There was no need to plan for an emergency, but now the minister introduces amendments which tighten up the regulations.
At a time when more people than ever need help, they are faced with these new restrictions. I support these restrictions, such as the restriction for extending the period of disqualification from three weeks to six weeks. In fact I wonder whether it should be a longer period. I remember years ago speaking to a gas station operator. He told me he had some youngsters, gas jockeys, working for him and they practically begged him to lay them off so that they could take the lumps of the two-week waiting period and have unemployment insurance coming to them and do what they wanted. That experience, I am sure, is repeated time and time again across the country. The system is abused by people who do not treat the program as unemployment insurance.
Now I should like to draw attention to the minister's statement in the folder that was distributed to all members. He said:
This amendment is being proposed because of the alarmingly high number of persons leaving their employment without good cause and refusing suitable employment. The number of voluntary quits has been averaging approximately 250,000 per year and job refusals for the first four months of 1975 would amount to an annual rate of 21,000. This is taking place despite the current unemployment situation, and the low ratio of job vacancies to the number of unemployed workers.
Thus it is clear that the present period of disqualification has not been sufficiently effective and needs to be increased. Workers' rights will continue to be fully protected; they will continue to be able to present their side of the case to their insurance agent, and have full recourse to the appeal system.

Unemployment Insurance Act
I ask, where were the departmental officials in 1971 when this program was planned? Do they have no capability for prediction? Could they not anticipate a little how this system would be abused? Did they have no ability to assess the possible way in which people could use that particular measure? This department has been profligate in its abuse of the taxpayers' money. It has been callous in not planning for this amendment at a time of low unemployment, and thus was not in a position to forewarn workers to prepare for the unpleasant prospects of unemployment. So, while this amendment is necessary, and in some way I suppose even welcome, it seems tragic indeed that it comes at a time when workers across Canada need unemployment insurance more than at any time in the last few years.
There is another reason why I question this legislation. I refer to the uneven administration of the program. The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) pointed out that the department has a curious ability to close a blind eye to the rip-off artists in the urban areas and then harry across the country the individual who tries to live within the rules.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I recieved a phone call from an elderly man in my riding a few months ago. He was approaching retirement years and thought he would do what others do. He thought he would take advantage of the unemployment insurance fund into which he had paid for the last many years of his employment. So, he quit his job and applied to the UIC. The UIC did what it does in respect of most unemployed people. It set about to answer the inquiries by prospective employers. So he was sent all over the valley to look at these job prospects provided by the UIC and Manpower. He is 55 years of age. He is a hardworking man who believes in the work ethic. He does not want to rip off the government. So he goes everywhere the Manpower office sends him. He tries to do the work. He does it.
Whenever a job is over he goes to the UIC and they send him to another job. The poor man cannot do what many other younger people are able to do. Finally he is working with a crew, a group of young bucks, and it begins to sprinkle rain. They go to the beer parlor because they do not want to get wet, and on the way they go to the social service to get a cheque to tide them over. This is an example of a man who deserves the benefit of unemployment insurance but he cannot collect it simply because he is honest.
Then I think of a lady who wrote me. She has poor vision and cannot drive. She has spent much time working in nursing homes. The only job that was available to her was 36 miles away. She was unable to find commuting facilities in order to get to this employment at the time when the nursing home wanted her. She applied for unemployment insurance because she could not take the job that was offered her.
I think of another man in retirement years. He had been working all his life in a sawmill. He was retired and wanted to do something else. He went to Quesnel and looked around for work. He was not part of the bureaucracy and was not someone ripping off the UIC. Therefore he did not know the procedure used by some other people to

rip off the UIC. He did not know that it was necessary to report every day when he went to Quesnel. The upshot is that he did not get work at Quesnel and did not receive the unemployment insurance benefits either because he did not follow the bureaucratic procedure outlined for him.
This man's case was taken to the appeal board. I am sure the members of the appeal board gave him as good a hearing as possible but, as the other hon. member pointed out, at no time was this man ever in a position where he could state his case personally to that tribunal and have it heard.
I have a very interesting letter from an employer of a man. This firm had a very good accountant who kept track of the man's work record. He began work on November 12, 1974. The last day he worked was December 30, 1974. Including those days, and excluding one week during which the shop was closed for Christmas, he could have worked some 30 days. The number of days in which he did work all or part of a day was 22. He thus missed some 26.7 per cent of the days on which he could have worked all or part of a day. The total available hours during those 30 days is computed to have been 240. He worked 169 Vt of these, representing only 70.5 per cent of the total available.
The letter states that this company is a manufacturing plant with an assembly-line operation and thus it is essential that each employee maintain a good attendance record. It further points out that each employee has this fact pointed out to him or her, and that there is no misunderstanding concerning what is expected. They say this man attended some 70 per cent to 75 per cent of the time when he was needed, and they found the level of attendance to be unsatisfactory in the extreme and stated that this accounted for the term used on the separation certificate, "unreliable". What does this man do when he is laid off? He goes to the unemployment insurance office. The next procedure obviously is that the employer has to fill out a questionnaire advising the Unemployment Insurance Commission of the reason for this man's suspension. They point out that he is unreliable.
As I look into it a little further I find that the man apparently told the foreman that he had been sick. I suppose that if he has been sick, there is good reason for him to have a very hyphenated employment record, but then if he has been sick it seems to me that he should not get unemployment insurance. If in fact he needs that kind of help-and I for one would not deny him such help- perhaps he needs some kind of social welfare, but certainly not unemployment insurance. That is one of the grave problems of the unemployment insurance program.
The next thing I notice about the amendment is the ambiguous phrase, to say the least, "who refuse suitable employment". I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what does "suitable" mean? In what kind of subjective terms can you describe that? Suitable in whose judgment? Is it in the judgment,of a man who is unemployed and, theoretically at least, looking for employment, or is it suitable to the Unemployment Insurance Commission?
Is it suitable in terms of the salary that is being offered? Is it suitable in terms of the working conditions, the kind
October 28, 1975

of job that is being offered, or the location of that job? What does suitable mean?
I suppose I have the disadvantage of many other members of the House to remember the "dirty 30's" when we lived in Saskatchewan at the height of the depression and, I suppose, the height of unemployment. I remember very clearly that every summer during those depression years my father would go to British Columbia and find seasonal work there. He would go to the lower mainland of the Fraser Valley and get a job haying, working in the tobacco fields or wherever there was work to be had. He would take his bicycle along and pedal around the Fraser Valley looking for work. It did not matter if the work was for a week or two hulling strawberries, hoeing hay, or doing anything that would provide employment and an income. Toward the end of the summer he would come back to Saskatchewan just in time for the harvest season and do day work in the fields of Saskatchewan.
Now when I think back to those times I cannot help but think that any of the jobs that my dad took during those depression years was suitable. It was not very suitable for him to leave for three months of the year to go out to a job paying $1 or $2 a day in British Columbia; it was not suitable to the rest of the family, perhaps even demeaning in many ways, but somehow it was not as demeaning as looking for a handout when he could work. Any job was suitable so long as it was honourable.
I remember that the hon. member for Okanagan-Kootenay (Mr. Johnston) pointed out that one of the main problems of UIC is that it is not even UIC any more. It is called insurance, but actually the problem is that it is treated as if it were social welfare. Perhaps it is time we drew the comparisons to show just how ludicrous and anachronistic the term has become. Again I still remember hearing the words of my friend from Labrador when he pointed out that this was a good insurance program. Let us compare it with an ordinary insurance program to see whether it really is insurance.
First of all, as the hon. member for Okanagan-Kootenay pointed out, insurance programs are voluntary; no one has to take out a life or fire insurance policy if he does not want to do so. Second, insurance policies are pooled investment for real emergencies, and I mean real emergencies not inconveniences. The startling difference is that insurance companies by the law of the land and the law of this government have to be actuarially sound. When we take a look at the unemployment insurance program we realize that if any private company operated an insurance program the way this government operates unemployment insurance, it would be drummed out of business.
Think of the billion dollars or more that the UIC program has in deficit and then wonder if it is possible to make an honest and accurate comparison actuarially between UIC and an insurance company. Furthermore, insurance policies are very specific. Any riders mean additional costs to the premiums and you pay for each one of those riders. It is the person who buys the insurance who makes that payment.
UIC has many riders and all of these are good, but not necessarily relevant to unemployment insurance. For example, sickness benefits are very good riders and I for one would not criticize the need to provide for the workers
Unemployment Insurance Act
for that eventuality when they are sick and need those benefits to carry them over through the period of sickness, but I do not know how you can correlate sickness benefits with other requirements of unemployment insurance, such as being available for work. I sense a constradiction there and I think it is time we called a spade a spade. There is a place for UIC and there is a place for social welfare, and I think the first priority of the government should be to draw a distinction between the two and make this into honest legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it may be relevant to point out that the present speaker on Bill C-69 is quite obviously female but rather less obviously an ex-chairman of the board of referees of the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
I feel that in human terms this is one of the most important pieces of legislation we have seen before the House in recent times. The ramifications of the proposals are considerable and complex, but at this time I will limit myself only to the consideration of clauses 14 and 16. As regards the former, I welcome it wholeheartedly.
In the past, sickness benefits have proven to be an administrative nightmare for the commission and the cause of very great frustration for the recipients. Under the old act the establishment of a sickness claim started what might be termed a clockwork action and in many cases, even though the recipient recovered and returned to work, the clock continued its futile course with resultant loss of benefit when benefits were again needed. This was all the more prevalent in the case of maternity benefits. The new act will allow the claimant to terminate the claim voluntarily or, to repeat the metaphor, to stop the clock. This innovation is, therefore, to be welcomed.
I mentioned the effect on maternity benefits. In this respect I would urge a further improvement. I refer to the pregnant woman who loses her employment because of labour disputes and therefore may not be entitled to receive maternity benefits because of section 44(1). Under this provision if a pregnant woman is a member of a grade or class of workers on strike, she is disqualified from receiving maternity benefits, especially in cases where the termination of the stoppage of work is not fulfilled when she becomes eligible for maternity benefits.
This section would appear to affect adversely the unionized woman, whereas it will have no bearing on her nonunionized sister. I see a possible dichotomy here, and I
8642

October 28, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
strongly recommend that the provisions of section 44(1) of the Unemployment Insurance Act be inapplicable in respect to maternity benefits.
Let us now consider clause 16 of Bill C-69, and its implications. On the surface it looks like a toughening up measure such as those long advocated by the people who will spend so much time and effort in decrying the weaknesses of the system that they have little energy to devote to the essential good offered to genuine recipients by the unemployment insurance scheme.
We must now ask ourselves: who will be the objects of the new and more stringent punitive measures? The answer is our youth and our women, two groups with whom I have particular sympathy. Why youth and women? It is because administrative statistics have proven conclusively that the rate of voluntary quitting is considerably higher among those two categories of employees.
Perhaps we should now ask ourselves why youth and women are more likely to quit. I believe the reasons are various and complex, and many of these are common to both groups. It would be very easy to assume that women are more likely than men to quit their jobs because of family responsibilities, but if they do, it is probable they do not ask the taxpayer to pay for their decision. In fact, of the women disqualified under the old act for reasons of non-availability, job refusal, and inadequate job search, a higher percentage of women with no dependants was registered than was the case for women with dependants. However, the difference was not so considerable as to constitute terms for debate.
In studying these and other results, it is of great importance to consider relevant aspects and to ask ourselves many questions such as: why do young people work? Why do women work? What is the importance of job satisfaction? Is job satisfaction itself a polemic which condemns too much, or a vision which promises too much?
A report entitled "Canadian Work Values" gives us the findings of the Department of Manpower and Immigration on a work ethic survey and a job satisfaction survey. I hope that in the national interest similar and ongoing initiatives will be undertaken. I suggest that in few other fields do attitudes change with such rapidity as in this. Consider, for example, the following statement: "60 per cent of Canadians still believe that a woman's place is in the home." This statement was recorded in 1975. We are also informed that this attitude is considerably less prevalent among higher educated and younger members of the population. It would be interesting, therefore, to see what is the more prevalent attitude in, say, another ten years.
There is a tendency for both women and men to believe that women should not have to work unless they choose to do so. Here again younger and more highly educated members of society feel they should.
What we are experiencing is quite obviously an evolution of attitudes. However, there is one area in which age and education make no difference. Regardless of age or education, women are more inclined than men to believe that women in general should supplement the household income.
Let us now consider the case of a woman with dependants. She has probably received much more formal educa-

tion than her mother. She has probably raised a family and has accumulated a wealth of experience as an administrator, economist, nurse, teacher, psychologist and arbitrator of disputes, to name only a few. She then decides to return to the labour market, probably to full time work, and if her children are young, more because of financial than any other need. What are her prospects? Is the labour force likely to recognize the full potential of this woman and justly evaluate her contribution? Unfortunately, the chances of her true worth being recognized are not good. All too often she will be offered jobs which are intellectually bankrupt. Because of her absence from the labour force during the time she looked after her children, her chances of promotion are limited, irrespective of her merit.
I believe that seniority in itself is a fine thing, but if it is used as the sole criterion for promotion at the expense of merit, then not only is it unrealistic, but it is positively dangerous to the economy as a whole.
This last point will also and perhaps particularly apply to our youth. We must remember that they too have an average education far superior to that of their fathers. Education widens one's horizons and also stimulates expectation. The resultant disillusionment and discouragement add another dimension to our mosaic of human frustration and miseries.
What of the working woman with no dependants, the one who preferred not to marry? Can she hope to achieve job satisfaction and promotion more easily than her married sister? The reality of the situation is not encouraging. If she is gentle and thoughtful, chances are she will be considered weak and quite expendable. To gain respect as a peer will almost inevitably require time, perseverance, and an extraordinary amount of patience.
If, instead, she is aggressive, she soon becomes the object of endless and often distasteful speculation, analysis, and innuendo. The recent case of an internationally successful female journalist is a prime example. During an interview published by Time magazine Signorina Fallaci was asked whether she is a lesbian. I know of few male writers since Oscar Wilde who have been subjected to such base sensationalism and whose private lives have been so dissected, and at the same time I fail to see what bearing her sexual preferences have on her undoubted ability as a journalist.
Administrative statistics have pointed out another interesting factor. It appears that the largest numbers of people who have abused the system come from clerical and related occupations. Here again I feel that employers must understand that if they hope to attract better educated personnel, they must make infinitely better efforts to provide in those jobs the challenge and prestige which education itself demands. Study has been devoted, and rightly so, to problems of alienation in assembly plants, but far too little is known of the numbing effects of months and years passed in the mindless atmosphere of a typing pool.
If there is one burning issue in this bill, an issue which will reverberate on the productivity of the entire nation, then surely it is the lesson that we are quickly learning that higher education will, of its very nature, lead to greater expectations. We cannot ignore these signs which
October 28, 1975

are already unmistakeably evident. Whether industry will accept the challenge and attempt to rectify the situation in the economic if not in the human interest, only time will tell. With this bill government will treat many of the symptoms but it certainly will not, and indeed cannot, cure the disease.
Many, many more thoughts could be and should be propounded on this argument but time simply does not permit. And so we ask why, despite compassion for and understanding of this problem facing our youth and women, will people such as I vote for and even advocate the punitive effects of this bill? It is quite simply because I feel that mature responsibility must, in the national and collective interest, take precedence over personal desires, legitimate though those desires may be.
Unemployment insurance is what it says-an insurance program much like any other. We will find people who do not like their houses but who would never dream of burning them down just to collect fire insurance. No, they will either tolerate them or look for alternative accommodation. So it should be with jobs and unemployment insurance.
In the interest of our national economy I would strongly urge employers to evaluate seriously the enormous wealth and human potential which, through lack of care and even minimal understanding, they continue to dissipate at an alarming rate.
At this very moment in time we are demonstrating an admirable and sincere concern for the conservation of natural resources. The time has come to include in the study of those resources the immeasurable riches of our undeveloped and under-employed human element.

Mr. Speaker, when we have the former minister of finance advocating changes in the operation of the Unemployment Insurance Commission on the grounds that "the cost to the government is becoming unwieldy" and admitting "that the act has some undesirable effects on work incentives", and when the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) tells us that "additional amendments are proposed to reduce some of the inequities and complexities which now exist," then I feel that we have the right to be gravely apprehensive about the operation of that commission.
I guess you could call it unwieldy when the increase of the cost of operating this act has risen by 150 per cent over the past year. Yet just three years ago we had the then minister of manpower and immigration telling us that "the extra costs present no problem to the government," and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) himself commenting on the $700 million deficit of that same year, saying that he "saw no scandal in that. . . What if the fund needs another $100 million or $200 million . .. ?"
When the cost to the government and to the contributors has increased threefold since that time, I say that we do have a problem and that we do have a scandalous situation.
At the very time that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration and the Prime Minister were not alarmed and saw no scandal, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) was warning that expenditures on this program were "very much out of hand from both the government's and the contributors' points of view." However, it was a case of a warning falling on deaf ears again.
Unemployment Insurance Act
The government continues to display the most astonishing lack of realism in the present situation but an abundance of it in hindsight. This hindsight of the Unemployment Insurance Commission difficulty bears a remarkable similarity to the government's presentation of price controls, more than a year after they were proposed by the party which I have the honour to represent.
Every member of this House must know that the largest number of complaints that he and his staff have to deal with are those which pertain to unemployment insurance matters. Such letters far outnumber those about any other problem on a continuous basis.
The most dominant areas of complaint, of criticism, of distress and dissatisfaction are with this branch of the Department of Manpower and Immigration. Day after day, at least until we had the postal strike, letters of anger and frustration with this commission flowed in. Constituents forward us volumes of correspondence which they have received from the UIC, and ask that we assist them to help to untangle the unintelligible mess. Applications whose format is unbelievably complicated, and letters which are thoroughly incomprehensible spew forth from this department. There are so many abuses and injustices in the Unemployment Insurance Act that it ought to be scrapped and a totally new concept undertaken.
The way in which the act has been mismanaged has caused it to deviate entirely from the meaning of insurance. It could more accurately be referred to as payment assurance. It is regarded by contributors as some sort of investment or savings account, and that if they have put money into it then they are entitled to get it back. It is about as logical as expecting to be reimbursed for premiums paid out for car insurance, if one chooses to drive one's car no longer. That is exactly the way many in the work force are thinking today. They feel that if they do not choose to work, then they are entitled to unemployment insurance benefits. The only thing that will ensure, Mr. Speaker, is that a number of people are going to try to beat the system, and it is being done with great success very often.
It is no longer true insurance against the time when one is unemployed, but another con game in which the smart operator can pick the public pocket. The serious job searcher often finds himself strangled in the maze of red tape. Many times a recipient of benefits is informed that he has been receiving benefits for which he does not qualify after all, and that he must repay the commission as much as $1,000 or there will be dire consequences. If there are cases of overpayment, of no entitlement, then why were benefits paid out for so long? Who is causing these errors?
Let us change the name, the concept, and the reality to an employment insurance commission-a commission that will encourage employment rather than one which has built-in disincentives to work. Only when it becomes more profitable to work and be gainfully employed than to live as well, or even better, when unemployed are we going to have a society in which the prestige of the work ethic will regain its rightful position as a desirable attribute. Work has become another four letter word, a dirty word in the vocabulary and thinking of too many people. And the present administration has fostered that attitude.

Unemployment Insurance Act
The puny amendments which are proposed to the act are a farce as far as alleviating the existing problems is concerned. The senior citizen is going to be ineligible for benefits, and the lower salaried will have to pay the same premium as many who are higher salaried, at a minimal saving to the government. Does the Minister of Manpower and Immigration consider discrimination against the elderly and the poor to be a reduction in inequity, because that is what will happen if the proposed regulations do go into effect?
There is absolutely no consistency or logic in the way in which UIC matters are handled or mishandled within the Department of Manpower and Immigration. It is absolutely essential that there be more co-operation and liaison between these two sectors so that they work in harmony. Is the problem of unemployment not linked with finding jobs or training people to new skills to fit developing opportunities?
Manpower is woefully inadequate in its purpose to create and locate jobs for those in need of them. Stress must be laid on getting those who are without work back into the work force as quickly as possible so that they can be a contributing unit to the welfare of Canada, rather than a drain upon it. Far too many are allowed to exist in relative comfort as they wait to have cheques delivered to them from schemes and plans spawned by the federal government.
The industrious contributors are becoming demoralized by carrying the double burden of higher premium payments to the UIC as well as increased taxes to the government to handle its share of the UIC pie. We may see the day when the workers become so demoralized at carrying the drones in our society that they will either rebel against the system or decide that it would be much smarter to join them. Then we will experience the ultimate strike.
The Unemployment Insurance Act is urgently in need of complete rebuilding. The time for band-aid remedies is long past. I heard the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo) extolling in her partisan way the supposed benefits of the present legislation. She expounded on the benefits of the Local Initiatives Program, benefits which I do not deny, as the program fulfills a need in society. But it is a stop gap program. Let me tell hon. members about an application made by the residents of the township of Flatbush in my constituency. They made an honest application to the government. They asked for only $2,873.

speechtext:
The request was too small, as my hon. friend says. Despite their honesty, they were refused. And why did they apply for this money? They needed it because the government has mismanaged the beef industry of this country. When the government is so involved in the beef industry that, in a two-year period, it introduces 29 different policies and programs, I say the government does not know what it is doing.
Before concluding may I refer to what my party said during the past election campaign, to show that it is consistent. I shall also refer to what the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) said in the present

debate. I shall refer to our policy commitments made in the 1974 campaign, and to the somewhat similar statement made by the hon. member for Hamilton West, to show that my party is consistent in its thinking, and that when we make commitments and statements we are willing to abide by them, which is more than you can say of the party opposite.
We, of the official opposition, still call for an independent inquiry into the operation of this act. Such an inquiry should examine the effectiveness of the act as now constituted, and its administration. It should envisage whether changes in the legislation are required, and investigate in particular the administration, with a view to maintaining an adequate program of unemployment insurance while avoiding disincentives to employment and excessive costs to contributors and taxpayers. This request is consistent with what we said during the election campaign and with my party's position. We feel, in short, that there should be a fully independent inquiry and not some sort of in-house inquiry about which the minister spoke, involving the unemployment insurance advisory council.
Further, we feel that there should be a fully independent inquiry into the workings of the Unemployment Insurance Act in order to determine whether it is an insurance scheme, a welfare scheme, or a combination of both, and if there are abuses, how to get rid of them. The inquiry should delve into the extent of disincentives, and recommend how best to remove them. The inquiry should be full blown and independent, and not something with which the minister can play hanky panky whenever he feels too much heat. In other words, we want an independent group to look at this serious matter.
The principle to which we should adhere is that any scheme such as the one we are considering should be a difficult one for any person to take advantage of, easy to administer, and easy to leave. In other words, it ought to be hard to get on the recipient rolls, and easy to get off. This, apparently, is not the case now, as this amending bill indicates.
By introducing disincentives to work the government has destroyed the work ethic. This is the result of a statement the Prime Minister made some time ago. He said that you do not have to work for money because there are other things in life which are so meaningful. That may be true, but it is the individual's responsibility to pay for those other things himself.
The hon. member for Hamilton West, my party's UIC critic, compared the situation in our country with that in the United States. His comparison was startling, and for that reason I shall quote a part of his speech made yesterday on October 27. He said, as reported at page 8572 of Hansard:
It is interesting to note that the United States, which has a population ten times the size of Canada's, spent $4 billion on unemployment insurance in 1973. On the other hand, we in Canada will spend approximately the same amount in 1975.
I have told the House what the government has done about the situation. My party has outlined what should be done. Unfortunately now, as in the past, our advice is falling on deaf ears.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as Bill C-69 which deals with unemployment insurance will become one of the most important bills this House will discuss during the present session, may I at this time congratulate colleagues in the Progressive Conservative Party who made such excellent contributions to this debate.
The subject of unemployment insurance and the operation of the commission have been of major concern to Canadians for a number of years. Clearly a major overhaul of our UIC program is long overdue. You could say that UIC recipients are almost like members of another profession. The commission in Canada has attracted thousands of Canadians to its doors. They come for the generous pay-outs. Some groups have formed UIC ski teams, and wear jerseys on which appear the words "UIC ski team." On the backs of other jerseys are printed the words, "Thanks, Pierre". I hope the minister is taking the necessary measures to stop UIC ski teams from being formed this winter, ski teams which will be financed by the Canadian taxpayer.
I shall now refer to a Gallup poll. It is a public opinion report on the UIC. The question the researchers asked was, "Do you think that the government has been strict enough, or not, in checking on applicants for unemployment insurance benefits?"
Canadians are watching for evidence of a program ensuring stricter control of unemployment insurance payments. While most people approve the increased benefits, provided they go to those who really need them, they give almost a three-to-one verdict that, at present, the screening of applicants for UIC payments is not satisfactory. Nationally 59 per cent hold this opinion, compared to 24 per cent who think the controls are satisfactory. Another 17 per cent are undecided.
These national levels of opinion are echoed in homes for all occupational segments in much the same degree. Conviction that supervision is not sound enough in accepting applicants is highest, however, among executive and professional workers and their families, with 61 per cent believing stricter controls are necessary, versus only 20 per cent who disagree. Argument is more closely debated in skilled and unskilled labour, with 63 per cent thinking supervision is too lax, and 27 per cent saying it is not. Only 10 per cent of those in the homes of labour are undecided about the issue, compared to 19 per cent among executives and professionals or sales and clerical workers, and 23 per cent among farmers and others.
I now touch on the work ethic. The work ethic in Canada has been destroyed by successive Liberal governments. No wonder it has been destroyed, considering the sorts of statements the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has made. For instance, the Prime Minister has said in the past, as reported in the Edmonton Journal of March 20, 1972:
I say that the most sacred law is that a man who lives in society should be able to enjoy his own possibilities to the maximum, but work is perhaps not the way to do it.
If we are lucky, we will move toward a leisure society where we will work less. The aim of man in society is not to work, it is to realize his own potential to the maximum.
Unemployment Insurance Act
He went even beyond this philosophical musing to the point of suggesting that there is nothing wrong with a deliberate decision to collect unemployment insurance rather than work.
"There should be no stigma attached to that. They paid their unemployment insurance premiums," Trudeau said of those who "prefer" not to work.
All this, of course, is pretty strong stuff from the leader of a country whose traditions are still deeply rooted in the work-oriented Protestant ethic.
To the extent that it suggests unemployment is rampant in Canada by the people's choice, it's also downright misleading. The... majority of Canada's . .. unemployed want a job now, and couldn't care less about some future ideal of a leisure society.
I wish to quote from a letter that I received from the vice-president of Firestone Tire & Rubber Company of Canada Limited about the difficulties they are encountering in hiring people to work for their company. I quote:
-our Plant Employment Office interviewed 2,521 potential plant employees for our Hamilton Tire Plant. Of that total, we hired 224 (acceptable candidates who were able to pass our medical examination). As of today's date, there are 110 of these 224 employees who are still working in our plant.
From our experiences, we have noticed a new breed of 'unemployed' person. When answering our newspaper advertisements, many applicants possess one of the following attitudes:
1.	They are content to sit through the interview and be shown the job and then not appear for the mandatory medical examination. We conclude that at least 10-15 per cent of the people tentatively hired refuse to accept the job in this manner.
2.	They are content to appear for the interview and behave in such a manner that would not be acceptable to any company. The candidate actually appears relieved when informed that he does not qualify to fill the job vacancy.
This certainly indicates that the job ethic in this country is deteriorating. He went on to say:
To us, this growing trend towards 'acceptable unemployment' is the direct result of relaxed regulations and attractive unemployment benefits.
How can we as a corporation or our employees as taxpayers cover these rising unemployment costs? As a corporation, we can hope to increase our productivity. But how can we do so when we cannot fill our vacant jobs with responsible people? How can we increase our productivity if we cannot attract applicants and retain them as employees when they can easily receive large sums of money from our government NOT TO WORK?
As for our employees, how can we increase their take-home pay to compensate for these new insurance payments when we are unable to increase our productivity and thus warrant these payroll increases?
It is our considered opinion that immediate action is necessary. We strongly recommend:
1.	The Unemployment Insurance Offices and the Manpower Offices should be integrated.
2.	The eight week qualifying period for insurance benefits should be increased to 20 weeks.
3.	And whereas the currently 20 hours a week in a week qualifies as one of the eight weeks required, this should be increased to 24 times the minimum wage of that jurisdiction concerned.
These last two proposals would eliminate from the Unemployment Insurance Plan some of the people who have only a casual or part-time attachment to the Canadian work force.
They are not only complaining and making suggestions, but attempting to do something about it. I hope the minister will pay particular attention to what I will now read. I think the vice-president has an excellent idea. He stated, and I quote:

October 28, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
Attached, please find a copy of a form letter that we are now using in co-operation with the Hamilton office of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. It is our intention to work closely with the Unemployment Insurance Commission and assist them and their staff to discover violators and habitual offenders that defraud Canadians of millions of tax-paid dollars.
We sincerely believe that government action should begin immediately. With every company reporting similar information to their local Unemployment Insurance Commission office and revised legislation amending the regulations, maybe then we could eliminate the abusers of the system. A concerted drive must be started at once to clear up this disorder. The time is now to once again elevate the status of the Commission, permitting it once again to assist those Canadians who honestly and deservedly need this assistance. Let's correct our worst energy crisis, "The lack of energy of the unemployment rolls".
I hope the minister will consider contacting all firms across Canada with regard to providing the Unemployment Insurance Commission with this type of information on offenders. Mismanagement of the Unemployment Insurance Commission has been of concern to the official opposition. I wish to give an example of our concern.
Here is a report of a $3.2 million loss in overpayments at an Unemployment Insurance Commission office. I quote:
More than a quarter of the $12.1 million in overpayments by the Unemployment Insurance Commission's Montreal office in the past two fiscal years has not been recovered, Manpower Minister Robert Andras said yesterday.
Overpayments in 1971-72 totalled $2.43 million, and $1.79 million of this was recovered. In 1972-73, overpayments were $9.68 million, of which $7.03 million was recovered.
This makes total overpayments of $12.11 million in the two fiscal years. The total recovered was $8.82 million, leaving an outstanding balance of $3.29 million.
It must be very time consuming and costly to recover these overpayments. That is an example of just one UIC office. If they were all totalled, I wonder what the amount would be.

I hope the minister is closing up those large holes. There are further shocking figures with regard to the Unemployment Insurance Commission. In 1974 Unemployment Insurance Commission payments made up 1.51 per cent of the gross national product. In 1975 total payments will amount to $4 billion, or 2.72 per cent of the gross national product. In other words, pay-outs will have increased by 186.3 per cent.
Here is where we are getting into trouble. In 1972 it was $1,871,808,000 with a government contribution of $717 million and employer-employee contributions amounting to $1,154 million. Listen to the figures for 1973. The total was $2,004,216,000. The government's contribution came to $573

million and the employer-employee contribution came to $1,431 million. Now for 1974 the figures are staggering. The total was $2,119,212,000, made up of $700 million in government contributions and $1,500 million in employer-employee contributions.
In 1975 it is expected that the total will reach $3,750 million. Of that, $1,750 million will be the government contribution, with $2 billion forthcoming from employer-employee contributions.
In closing, if Bill C-69 goes to committee a concerted effort must be made by the members and the minister to find out how the Unemployment Insurance Commission can be made self-sustaining financially, and not obliged to call continually for increases in premiums which amount to just another tax on the Canadian public.

Mr. Speaker, I am amazed that my friends on the benches opposite have not taken this sterling opportunity to speak out on this important bill. I am sure Canadians living in their constituencies are every bit as upset and alarmed at this horrible mess called the UIC as are Canadians in constituencies represented by members who support this party.
The Unemployment Insurance Commission can only be called a mess. Indeed that is too gentle a word to describe the operations of this program. If one had to identify any single government program or government action which was more responsible than another for the near defeat of the Liberal party in October, 1972, it would be the Unemployment Insurance Act brought in by the present Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey).
In a sense I suppose I owe the government a vote of thanks because there is no question but that the issue of the Unemployment Insurance Commission made it much easier for me to get elected for the first time in 1972. The famous Unemployment Insurance Commission ski team T-shirts were very much in evidence in my constituency, in the town of Banff as well as on the ski hills. The evidence of rip-offs at the expense of this scheme was very prevalent and known to a large number of people in the constituency and the backlash of that stupid government legislation contributed greatly to my victory in 1972. I should like to think that my victory in 1974 was more attributable to the record of the member in the previous period.
It is too bad it has taken so long for the government to respond by bringing in even these modest amendments to the act. Members opposite did recognize they had created a monster-that the act they had amended in 1970 was, in fact, a monster. The Speech from the Throne in January, 1973, promised amendments, but under the threats of the then leader of the New Democratic Party the government did not feel it could muster sufficient courage to implement that promise, feeling no doubt that though it would cost the Canadian public a few hundred million extra dollars to do so, the Canadian public would willingly pay that sum in order to maintain a Liberal government in office. I am sure that at this point in time the Canadian people, especially after hearing the Thanksgiving Day message, must have second thoughts about this.

The change which was made removing the limit was, really, a shocking mistake. Removing the limit on the amount the treasury could contribute to the fund opened up frightening possibilities, and many of us in this party regret we did not put up a more vigorous opposition to that particular amendment.

The Canadian people have now had four years in which to judge the effectiveness of the legislation since the previous amendment in 1971. Indeed, there are a lot more Canadians who are capable of forming opinions about the Unemployment Insurance Commission as a direct result of their own experience. In 1971 unemployment was running at 5.9 per cent, and roughly 495,000 were unemployed. Today, the figure is running at 7.2 per cent and some 800,000 Canadians are clients of the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
