subtopic: OLYMPIC GAMES-REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE MEDALLIONS MINTED IN CANADA
OLYMPIC GAMES-REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE MEDALLIONS MINTED IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tonight I intend to pursue my question to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) of October 27 dealing with the possibility of minting Olympic
Adjournment Debate
commemorative medallions to supplement the drastically sagging sales of Olympic silver coins.
The concern which obviously arises in this connection stems from the fact that private Canadian mints such as the Lombardo mint in Quebec, the Jacques Cartier mint in Toronto, and others which did not get a chance to bid on the commemorative medals were all bypassed by COJO in favour of a Swiss firm whose so-called Canadian subsidiary Suissecon Watch Company Limited is found not to be an incorporated company in either the Dominion of Canada or any of the provinces.
The sad part of the matter is that the example just given is only one of the many ways in which qualified Canadian firms have been effectively shut out and prevented from taking part in the production and development of products for the Olympic Games.
I realize that the government's answer to my request for intervention by the federal government for the benefit of Canadian manufacturers and Canadians in general will be that COJO's business affairs are out of the federal government's jurisdiction. Let me point out, however, that the Olympic coin program is totally under the jurisdiction of the federal government and that the commemorative medal proposals are directly connected with the coin program. Allow me for the sake of clarification to quote, Mr. Speaker, from a coin program tender signed jointly by Gerry Snyder, vice-president/revenue of COJO, and Mr. Austin Page, managing director of the Olympic coin program, directly responsible to the federal government:
A description of the marketing program you are prepared to implement for the distribution and sale of coins and medals in the United States, Canada and overseas. This description should include order of magnitude marketing budgets proposed for each element of the marketing program and estimates of anticipated sales of coins and medals for each element. It should be noted that sales of coins should be restricted to the United States while sale of medals should be worldwide. The organizing committee and the coin program in this respect will develop with you a list of potential international distributors of the official medals.
You would have noted, Mr. Speaker, that reference in the quote is made not only to Olympic coins but to medals as well, which go hand in hand with the coins. There is no question, therefore, that to me this reflects the fact that since the medals and coins are part of the same category under the coin program, which is the sole responsibility of the federal government, it is the economic and moral duty, indeed the obligation, of the federal government to take immediate steps to intervene in COJO's decision to have these and other products manufacted abroad without giving Canadian businessmen a fair opportunity to manufacture them.
This is just one of the many reasons why I have today called upon the government to initiate a full scale public inquiry into the organization and conduct of the 1976 Olympics, in order to reduce any further unnecessary expenditure and so that public confidence in the games will be restored and the games assured of the success Canadians wish them to have.
As I have said, this is just one of the many reasons why an investigation is necessary. The fact that the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) does not even know the man who

October 28, 1975
Adjournment Debate
will head the mammoth security forces, estimated to cost the federal taxpayer $90 million, is another reason. The fact that some maniacal terrorists are planning to use the Olympics as the stage for their political insanities is another reason. The fact that the cost of the games themselves are expected to reach an estimated $1 billion, compared with the original estimate of $310 million, is another. The fact that the direct federal commitments will reach, in my opinion, $250 million before the end of the Olympic Games, is yet another.
For example, I have here figures in a document produced by the immigration department, figures that to this date have not been made public, estimating that $3.2 million is reserved in that department to pay for Olympic immigration over and above the regular budget. The fact that there presently exists six million pieces of finished and unsold silver coins in the vaults of the Mint to the value of approximately $50 million is another reason.
In the time allotted me this evening I do not have time to expound on all the other reasons why it is necessary to have an investigation. The fact of the matter is that the time has come for the federal government to come clean with the people of Canada by making all the obvious irregularities public through an inquiry such as I have proposed; and perhaps even at this late date we as Canadians can end up being proud of hosting the Olympic Games.

TRANSPORT-DATE OF IMPLEMENTATION OF RECOMMENDATION THAT COMMISSION PORTS GIVE GRANTS IN LIEU OF TAXES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the past year I have been drawing the matter of the Surrey container port facilities to the attention of the Minister of Transport. I would hope tonight that the parliamentary secretary would speak directly to the issue of the Scott report and its recommendations, and give us

more than simply departmental generalizations and public relations statements on this matter, because this is a matter of great import to the thousands of people in the lower mainland of British Columbia.
I have spoken to the former minister, in this forum as well as in personal conversation, about the matter, and on a number of occasions he has assured me that the Scott report will be the final answer to the problems of the municipalities as they relate to the commission port facilities across Canada. I have been assured on many occasions that the Scott report will be included in the recommendations and that the commission ports will pay grants in lieu of taxes.
The container port facilities operated by the Fraser River Harbor Commission of New Westminster were opened last December in Surrey. I should first of all compliment the commission on the excellent facilities, on the excellent operation, the very efficient operation and, I might add, the prosperous operation. It is making money. That is something to be commended. When any government operation makes money I think we should stop and take note, especially in contrast to the facilities of the National Harbours Board. As I have said, these facilities were opened last December, almost a year ago now. All we have had in the meantime is a vague assurance that something will be done, that the Scott report will be handed down and that it will be the answer. I should like to point out to the minister what this kind of dalliance means to the taxpayers of Surrey.
I have with me an estimate from the municipal engineer of Surrey concerning what it will cost Surrey to make sure that the access facilities to the container port facility will be up to the standards required. It will have to upgrade a number of roads. There will have to be Robson and Plywood roads with an asphalt overlay at a cost of $40,000. There will have to be 2,100 feet of two roads, Tannery- Scott to Timberland reconstructed at a cost of $125,000. There will have to be 900 feet of Timberland and Old Yale covered with an overlay at a cost of $60,000.
There you have a total cost for the roads alone of $225,000. This is no small item when you consider the soil conditions in the area. They are extremely poor. There is a very high water content and the soil in that area is peat. There is a large engineering cost involved in this project. Since it is a port facility it is obvious that on the low land of the river there will have to be drainage. The reconstruction of the ditch enclosures for these facilities will represent something in the area of $420,000. To bring up the access and drainage facilities will cost $645,000 to the taxpayer of Surrey. So much for the expenses to the taxpayers, but on the other side of the ledger is the revenue that should be accruing to the taxpayer, and there are four pieces of property involved in this facility.
The taxes that should be coming to the municipality of Surrey each year beginning in 1975, followed by the increments, should be $205,851.28. Those are the projected taxes for 1975. When you combine the lost revenue with the projected expenses, you have the total of $850,851.28. This is what it means to the taxpayer of Surrey municipality because this government had made promises and had said
October 28, 1975

recommendations will be coming which would take the pressure off.
If the government is really concerned about equity, justice, and fairness, then I think it will make the recommendations of the Scott report known to the Canadian people and to the Surrey municipality, and will ensure that the government there will receive the tax dollars it deserves so that it can service the facilities it has within its boundaries.
I underscore the fact that we welcome the facilities which are excellent and job producing, but if we want to make them the kind of facilities they should be in terms of services, then it will cost the taxpayer; and if the federal government insists on putting facilities within the boundaries of a municipality which create a burden to the taxpayers, it is only right that it share in the burden of paying for services for those facilities.

Mr. Speaker, as I begin let me say that I appreciate hearing the hon. member's kind words about the quality of the facility that has been installed in this case. I hope that in my remarks this evening I will be able to shed a little more light on some of the questions which he has raised.
As the House knows, last June the Scott report recommended that the government pull together the administration of ports in this country into a more unified system. It also recommended that further study be done on the financial administration of ports.
The government has since announced its new policy to create a Canadian ports commission as well as some 25 semi-autonomous local port commissions. This commission would be within the marine administration of the Ministry of Transport, and would have responsibility to exercise the federal mandate for ports, including ports planning, capital development, and financial control. To bring this policy into being, a ports task force has been appointed to prepare instructions for the drafting of new legislation, and to provide answers to a number of financial and organizational questions, including the matter of grants in lieu of taxes.
On the basis of this task force report the government will bring forward a new Canada ports act for consideration by parliament. As the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) stated in the House, it is not possible to determine the exact timing of the changes which have to be made, in particular with reference to the changes mentioned by the hon. member. Implementation of the new policy and of the new financial arrangements, however, will immediately follow the passage of the required legislation.

subtopic: GRAIN-ALLEGATION WHEAT BOARD PUTS EXPORT GRAIN IN NON-BOARD CATEGORY AND DISTRIBUTES TO EASTERN FARMERS BUT NOT WESTERN FARMERS
GRAIN-ALLEGATION WHEAT BOARD PUTS EXPORT GRAIN IN NON-BOARD CATEGORY AND DISTRIBUTES TO EASTERN FARMERS BUT NOT WESTERN FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 4, 1975, I put a question to the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) that dealt with a distribution discrepancy.
Apparently non-board wheat can be made available to eastern farmers but not to those in the west. This has been brought to my attention by several concerned groups in
Adjournment Debate
western Canada. They have stated that they cannot purchase non-board grain at non-board grain prices but what they can purchase is grain from the Wheat Board at Wheat Board prices. However, in the east Wheat Board grain is turned over into the category of non-board grain and the non-board grain sells for considerably less than the Wheat Board grain. This is just one area in which I feel that there is a certain amount of discrimination in regard to the grain situation as it now exists in Canada.
There are several other matters with which I wish to deal in making this brief presentation because there are many areas of dissatisfaction in western Canada, and I should like to mention a few of these this evening. I am aware that in the few moments the hon. gentleman has to respond to what I have to say, he will state that this is not the case, but let me remind hon. members that that is exactly what was stated throughout the 1974 election in regard to wage and price controls. How quickly hon. members opposite change their minds, and how quickly they can change their opinions to suit their personal expediency.
While dealing with this issue I do not just wish to deal with the narrow aspects of it, but I should like to include some other areas in which western people feel they have not received a fair deal in confederation. This feeling has been constant throughout history, and is there any wonder that there is such ill feeling when they in the western regions have been looked upon as a colonial state for the purpose of supporting the golden triangle of Ontario?
Agricultural economies throughout the world have always been poor. Consider the southern hemisphere in all the developing nations. Consider every industrial nation of the world, and where there are within them agricultural regions those are the poor regions, and yet agriculture is the most essential of all industries. Consider Canada. The agricultural regions are poor unless they have some other resource. That has been the history of the prairies and the maritime provinces of this country.
To some Canadians the west has been a source of agitation recently. Some have made the comment that Alberta is trying to get out of confederation. They saw one issue correctly. There is agitation, and there is a feeling of uneasiness, but they read the signs wrongly and gave the wrong interpretation to the facts of the matter. What is really happening is that the west is trying to get into confederation. That is what I hope I can convey through the parliamentary secretary to the minister this evening.
Just to give a bit of an over view on how the regions of this country have been treated by the federal government for the past 100 years, central Canada has had the protection of tariffs. The colonial regions paid more than did central Canada for textiles, automobiles, farm machinery, and manufactured products. This is very nice for central Canada, but the producers see it as pickpocketing. If we are truly a confederation, then the confederation must be two way. If we are to have cheap oil across the country and if we are to have cheaper food products across the country, then the federal government must consider the well being of all of Canada and not just that of central Canada. It must talk of Canada as being a whole nation from sea to sea.

If the government really feels it has been responsive to the regions, then we can ask legitimate questions. I ask hon. members opposite how it was that they accepted the fact that the great depression lasted a full three years longer on the prairies than it did in central Canada?
Let me ask hon. members opposite to justify why western Canada pays twice as much to bring manufactured rapeseed back from Toronto to Lethbridge than it does to ship raw rapeseed per ton from Lethbridge to Toronto? Why is it that iron and steel products from Toronto are cheaper when shipped to Vancouver than when shipped to Saskatoon?
